title: Developing acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties to expand faba bean adaption.
description:
Faba bean production in Australia is constrained by soil acidity, particularly in Western Australia, South Australia, southern New South Wales and parts of Victoria, where acidic soils reduce root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop vigour and grain yield. Soil acidity also limits the expansion of faba bean into otherwise suitable production environments. While liming remains an important soil management practice, sub-surface acidity is often difficult, slow and costly to remediate, creating a need for complementary genetic solutions that improve crop performance and profitability on affected soils.
Recent GRDC investments have successfully delivered acid-tolerant rhizobia for faba bean, improving nodulation and nitrogen fixation under low pH conditions. However, the effectiveness of these inoculants depends on successful plant-rhizobia interactions, and current elite faba bean germplasm remains poorly adapted to acid soils (pH (CaCl2) <5.0). Developing acid-soil-tolerant varieties is therefore essential to fully realise the benefits of improved rhizobia strains and maximise productivity in acidic soil environments.
This four-year investment will accelerate the development of acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties by delivering the germplasm, genetic knowledge and breeding tools required to support long-term genetic improvement. The investment will identify and validate novel sources of acid soil tolerance from Australian and international germplasm, improve understanding of the physiological, biochemical and genetic mechanisms underpinning tolerance, and translate these discoveries into practical breeding outcomes for Australian faba bean breeding programs. Controlled-environment screening, field-based validation and modern genomic approaches will identify and characterise traits associated with improved performance on acidic soils, including traits linked to root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop establishment and yield. Activities should address both surface and sub-surface soil acidity and generate robust, field-relevant data to support breeding and selection decisions across target production environments.
A key component of the investment will be the development of validated high-throughput phenotyping methods, screening protocols and molecular markers that enable efficient selection for acid soil tolerance. These tools will support more rapid and cost-effective identification and deployment of favourable alleles within breeding pipelines, accelerating genetic gain for adaptation to acidic soils. Breeder-ready germplasm will incorporate novel acid-soil-tolerance alleles and demonstrating improved performance under acidic soil conditions, with a target yield advantage of at least 10% over benchmark varieties grown on acid soils of pH (CaCl2) below 5.0. Germplasm should be validated across representative production environments and supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and marker datasets to facilitate immediate use in breeding programs.
Strong collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to guide trait prioritisation, validation environments, phenotyping approaches and deployment pathways, ensuring outputs align with breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the genetic resources, screening tools and knowledge required to develop future faba bean varieties with improved adaptation to acid soils, enhanced yield stability and increased productivity. These advances will complement existing soil amelioration practices and acid-tolerant rhizobia, support expansion into suitable regions, improve reliability on acid soils and strengthen the competitiveness and sustainability of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: Enhancing faba bean seed colour and seed size uniformity to increase the value of faba beans and reduce risk of classifi
description:
Faba bean is an important Australian pulse crop and export commodity, supplying premium food and feed markets where visual grain quality is a key determinant of market access, classification and value. Buyers place strong emphasis on seed coat colour, colour retention and seed size uniformity, with these traits directly influencing grading outcomes, market acceptance and the price received throughout the value chain. Variability in visual grain quality, together with seed coat darkening during storage and handling, can increase the risk of downgrades, reduce grower returns and weaken Australia’s competitive advantage in premium export markets.
Although visual grain quality is known to have a strong genetic component, the biological, biochemical and environmental factors influencing seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity are not well understood. Australian breeding programs currently have limited access to the genetic resources, molecular markers and high-throughput phenotyping tools needed to efficiently improve these traits. Recent advances in genomics, artificial intelligence, digital imaging and data analytics provide new opportunities to accelerate genetic gain and develop more effective breeding solutions.
This four-year investment will develop the knowledge, genetic resources and breeding-enabling tools required to improve seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity in Australian faba beans. The investment will investigate the genetic, physiological, biochemical and environmental drivers underlying visual grain quality, including the mechanisms responsible for seed coat oxidation and post-harvest darkening. Activities should consider both genetic and non-genetic contributors to trait expression, including the effects of storage conditions, handling practices and environmental influences on grain quality outcomes.
A key component of the investment will be the development and validation of modern phenotyping and analytical tools to enable routine selection for visual grain quality traits. This includes the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital imaging and high-throughput phenotyping approaches to objectively measure seed coat colour stability, seed size uniformity and other commercially important visual attributes. Identification and incorporation of valuable genetic variation for improved seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity will enable development of breeder-ready germplasm for use in Australian faba bean breeding programs. Germplasm should demonstrate measurable improvements in visual grain quality traits and be supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and validated molecular marker datasets to facilitate rapid integration into breeding pipelines.
Strong and ongoing collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to help guide trait prioritisation, phenotyping methods, validation activities and deployment pathways. This will ensure outputs are aligned with market requirements and breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into crossing blocks, breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the germplasm, molecular markers, phenotyping tools and knowledge required to accelerate the development of future faba bean varieties with improved visual grain quality, greater market suitability and reduced risk of classification downgrades. These advances will help maintain existing market premiums, improve storage and marketing flexibility, protect Australia's reputation as a supplier of high-quality faba beans and strengthen the long-term competitiveness and value of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: ACRCP6-Integrated Rust Initiative: Program 3. Integrated Disease Management and Extension
description:
Cereal rust diseases continue to pose a significant and evolving threat to Australian wheat, barley and oat production. Wheat rust alone costs the Australian grains industry $147 million pa when controlled with genetics and current management practices, but predicted losses are close to $1.7 billion pa if no control occurs (Murray and Brennan, 2009). Rust pathogens are highly adaptable and have repeatedly overcome deployed genetic resistance and chemical control options, resulting in yield losses, increased fungicide use and rising production costs for growers. While the Australian Cereal Rust Control Program (ACRCP) has delivered strong outcomes over multiple phases, the increasing complexity of pathogen evolution (E.g. Yr15 virulent pathogen and BGYR pathogen evolution), fungicide sensitivity, loss of access to chemistry risk and climate driven disease pressure requires a more integrated and future focused investment approach.
The next phase will bring these activities together in a coordinated national initiative. It will strengthen rust surveillance, accelerate the development and use of durable genetic resistance, and improve integrated disease management across production systems. Expanding the program beyond wheat to include barley and oats will allow proven approaches and lessons to benefit the broader grains industry.
The Australian Cereal Rust Control Program Phase 6 (ACRCP6) – Integrated Rust Initiative will build on existing capability while addressing gaps in coordination, efficiency and preparedness for emerging rust threats. By supporting more durable crop resistance, responsible fungicide use and better-informed decisions by breeders, advisers and growers, the initiative aims to reduce the long-term cost and impact of cereal rust.
This procurement is specifically for the Integrated Disease Management (IDM) and Extension component of ACRCP6. GRDC is seeking a provider to identify priority rust management gaps, develop and update practical IDM strategies, and translate surveillance, crop resistance, seasonal risk and fungicide stewardship information into timely resources and advice for growers and advisers. The work will support more effective rust management, reduce reliance on reactive fungicide use and improve the grains industry’s long-term resilience.

title: Establishing pigeon pea as a summer pulse crop in the Northern Region
description:
Description:
The northern grains industry is seeking a more reliable summer legume option for hotter, drier farming environments where current commercial options are limited. While mungbean and soybean are well-established in some parts of the northern region, their higher water requirements and sensitivity to heat, seasonal stress and limited stored soil moisture can make them less dependable in lower-rainfall areas. This limits growers’ ability to confidently include a summer legume in rotations, reducing opportunities to improve system diversity, nitrogen inputs and overall farming system resilience.
Pigeon pea has been identified as a potential crop to address this gap. Its drought tolerance, resilience in constrained soils and ability to withstand more extreme seasonal conditions make it a strong candidate for environments where mungbean and soybean are not consistently reliable. Early GRDC-supported work has demonstrated that pigeon pea can be grown successfully across initial target environments in southern Queensland, central Queensland and northern New South Wales, and has helped identify promising genetic material and preliminary management considerations.
This investment will engage a delivery partner to design and deliver a coordinated field trial, extension and industry development program that builds on previous GRDC-supported pigeon pea work. The program will validate key agronomic practices across northern farming environments, generate evidence on yield potential, grain quality and farming system fit, and develop practical management guidance for growers and advisers. The delivery partner will also extend findings through targeted engagement with growers, advisers, industry and supply chain stakeholders, and provide the data and samples needed to support market development, future pre-breeding priorities and minor use permit applications. This investment is intended to be GRDC’s primary mechanism for improving the profitability, industry readiness and adoption of pigeon pea as a viable summer pulse option for the Northern Region.
Outcome:
<span">By 30 September 2030, growers in the target region of south-west and central Qld have the confidence to plant and profitably manage pigeon pea across 30,000ha thereby achieving a minimum viable industry.
Outputs.
Output 1.
Title: Develop tailored agronomic practices to achieve full yield for pigeonpea grown in Queensland in North NSW.
Description:
By October and annually thereafter, the investment will establish field experiments ti validate key agronomic practices tailored to pigeonpea production across Queensland and northern NSW. These practices will build on previous GRDC research and incorporate novel management tactics to better define yield potential across different cropping systems and environments. Experiments will be conducted across the GRDC sub-regions of NE NSW, NW NSW, SE QLD, SW QLD and Central QLD.
Field trials will evaluate the following:
- - Yield potential and ideal growing traits for each region/climate.
- - Agronomic management options e.g. sowing date, sowing configurations, fertiliser application, irrigation, etc.
- - Producing optimal grain standards for end users.
- - Pest management guidelines.
- - Disease critical thresholds.
- - Legacy implication of implementing pigeonpea into a farming systems e.g. nitrogen legacy.
The service provider will be required to work closely with GRDC’s CP&I team through AKC2507-001SAX to ensure project data is available to support minor use permit applications, particularly for desiccation, as well as insect and weed management issues.
The field experiments to develop key agronomic management plans tailored for each sub-region, providing clear guidance for growers to adopt and implement in their cropping systems.
Output 2.
Title: Extension and adoption of best management practices.
Description:
The project will deliver a coordinated extension and adoption pathway annually between 2027 and 2030. The pathway will be developed with early adopter insights and tailored to growers, advisers and supply chain participations across the northern sub-regions. Activities will move beyond field days and publications to maintain grower interest and momentum throughout the project, support peer-to-peer learning, build adviser capability and strengthen broader industry confidence in pigeonpea as a viable summer pulse option.
The activities may include:
- - Technical grower management plans tailored to each sub-region and cropping system.
- - Regional demonstration sites and annual field walks at key experiment locations to sow best management practice under commercial conditions.
- - Peer-to-peer learning activities, including grower case studies, paddock-based discussions, decision-support resources and targeted updates that enable advisers to support adoption.
- - Ongoing communication through GRDC GroundCover, digital media, videos, podcasts, social media and seasonal updates.
- - Engagement with supply chain participants, seed suppliers, marketers and potential end users to build confidence in production, grain quality requirements and market pathways.
- - Broader industry engagement with relevant grower groups, agribusiness networks and partner organisations to support coordinated adoption and reduce the risk of fragmented industry development.
Output 3.
Title: Gather supporting information for market requirement and pre-breeding priorities.
Description:
By June 2030, the investment will generate and apply key data and project findings to inform grain industry requirements and priorities future pre-breeding needs for pigeonpea. Building on previous desktop studies and exploratory work, the project will validate Australia’s capacity to produce commercial quantities of pigeonpea for human consumption and feedstock markets.
The project will work with industry participants to provide the samples, data and evidence required to inform grain quality standards. MRLs and priority pre-breeding targets for future investments.

title: Proof of Concept Funding - Call 2 2026
description:
Proof-of-concept (PoC) activities are a critical step in the development of any innovation. It is at this stage that evidence demonstrating the feasibility of an innovative concept is generated, typically through experimentation or pilot projects. PoC investments are usually time-sensitive, relatively low in capital and set the scene for future development plans, typically involving a significant increase in the financial resources as well as technical sophistication required to take the innovation all the way to adoption and impact.
The Grains Proof of Concept Funding program focusses on research activities that provide critical information to give confidence in future research and development investment such as early prototype development and/or validation, in planta proof-of-concept studies in relevant models, controlled environment trials, in-silico modelling, and analysis to support future investment decisions such as use-case analysis, and feasibility studies. It will also seek to support cross industry/discipline technology translation activities to encourage the application of existing research and development from adjacent industries, within the grains industry. The Grains Proof of Concept Funding program is not intended to support derisking commercial activity.
Strategic Alignment
GRDC is calling for innovative RD&E proposals in all Focus Areas identified in GRDC’s Research, Development & Extension Plan 2023-28. GRDC welcomes all Focus Area aligned innovative proposals, however, the Focus Areas will be prioritised through evaluation criteria.
Activities will support a plan for research and development activities to realise the concept and deliver the benefits to Australian grain growers.

title: Optimising agronomy of irrigated crops to enhance profit per megalitre of water
description:
The work will synthesise evidence from previous GRDC irrigated agriculture investments and assess priority opportunities to improve profitability from irrigated cropping systems, with a focus on maximising profit per megalitre of irrigation water rather than yield or water-use efficiency alone.
The analysis must consider the agronomic and economic drivers that influence irrigated crop decisions, including water availability, water price, input costs, seasonal conditions, crop potential, crop end use, rotations, and whole-farm water allocation. It must also assess how irrigation delivery systems and practices, including surface or furrow and pressurised sprinkler systems, interact with soil physical constraints and crop management factors to influence crop performance, input efficiency and profit per megalitre. For this procurement, irrigated crops primarily refers to grain crops within GRDC’s remit. The analysis should also consider how these crops compete with, complement or interact with other irrigated enterprises, including rice, cotton, forages and mixed farming systems, where relevant to whole-farm water allocation and opportunity costs.
The successful tenderer will be required to review existing irrigation and crop decision-support tools, identify whether they are meeting grower needs, and assess whether practical economic tools or decision frameworks are required to support more confident and timely irrigation research investment decisions across winter and summer cropping scenarios.
The final output will be a clear, evidence-based report that identifies priority research gaps, high-leverage agronomic opportunities, and practical recommendations to guide future GRDC investment in irrigated agronomy at national and regional scales.

title: Understanding barriers and enablers to IPM adoption in Australian grains
description:
Australian grain growers are managing pests in an increasingly complex and constrained environment. Key challenges include increasing insecticide resistance, changing access to crop protection products, regulatory and market pressures, emerging and episodic pest threats, and the need to protect beneficial insects and biological control services while preserving the effectiveness of available chemistry.
GRDC has previously invested in integrated pest management (IPM) adoption, extension and research into the factors that influence practice change across a range of grain-growing regions and pest systems. This provides an important foundation, but much of the earlier adoption work was undertaken before the current level of pressure from insecticide resistance and chemical access constraints, and before more recent changes in how growers and advisers access information and make pest-management decisions.
GRDC is seeking a suitably qualified provider or multidisciplinary team to undertake an independent opportunity analysis examining the barriers, enablers and pathways influencing practical IPM adoption in Australian grain systems. The analysis will draw on existing evidence, current and previous GRDC and industry investments, available tools and resources, relevant experience from other agricultural industries and international cropping systems, and the perspectives of growers, advisers, researchers, extension and adoption practitioners, and other relevant stakeholders.
The work must consider the technical, behavioural, advisory, commercial and broader system-level factors influencing grower and adviser practice change. It must establish a contemporary understanding of current IPM adoption capability, barriers and enabling conditions; assess what has changed since previous IPM adoption and extension investments; and identify the audiences, circumstances and delivery approaches where future effort is most likely to improve practical adoption outcomes.
GRDC requires practical, evidence-based and decision-ready recommendations to guide the design of future research, development, extension and adoption investments in IPM. The work is intended to focus on adoption and practice-change pathways rather than undertake a detailed technical review of individual pests or pest-management tactics. Where technical limitations are affecting adoption, these should be identified as matters that may require further research and development.

Stage 2, subject to future Commonwealth approval, will include offshore execution activities, including recovery of spools, jumpers, flying leads, flexibles, umbilicals, subsea structures, mooring lines and suction anchors, together with transport and load-in or offloading of recovered materials.
The procurement also includes Optional Scope for title surrender activities and seabed restoration, if required. The initial contract award is expected to authorise Stage 1 only. This is an open tender invitation to Tenderers who hold eligible surface water rights in the New South Wales (NSW) Border Rivers catchment to submit a Tender Response for the sale of water rights (either whole or in part) to the Australian Government.
The Australian Government (represented by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (the Department)) is seeking to purchase an estimated 3.68 GL/y long term diversion limit equivalence (LTDLE) of surface water from the NSW Border Rivers.
Water that is purchased through this ATM will contribute to bridging the gap to the Sustainable Diversion Limits under the Murray–Darling Basin Plan 2012 (Basin Plan).
The Department intends to consider Tender Responses submitted during the Tender Window, between the time the ATM is released until 11:00 am local time in the Australian Capital Territory on Thursday 11 March 2027 (Closing Time) unless otherwise advised by the Department.
The Department may choose to stop considering Tender Responses earlier, for example if the required volumetric targets under this ATM are achieved. This will be communicated via notice on AusTender and the Department’s website (www.dcceew.gov.au/watertender), with the Tender360 online submission portal closed for submission.
Important: This is a long duration open tender with a rolling evaluation process. Tender Responses can be submitted at any time during the Tender Window (unless the Department stops considering Tender Responses as outlined above), and Tender Responses will be assessed as they are received throughout the Tender Window (noting that such assessment may continue after the Tender Window Closing Time).

title: Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre Lead Partner
description:
The Commonwealth is undertaking two separate but related approaches to market (ATM) in parallel to support the establishment of the OET DRC and the delivery of its Inaugural Research Projects (IRPs). The processes being undertaken include:
a. ATM ID 13016 Lead Partner Request For Tender (RFT) (this RFT): to engage a supplier as a Lead Partner to provide research leadership and expertise at the program and project level for the OET DRC; and
b. ATM ID 13457 Contributing Partner Request For Information (RFI) (separate process): to engage with the market for the purposes of:
(i) understanding market capability and potential suppliers that align with, and have interest in, research related to the OET DRC; and
(ii) informing the development and conduct of this Lead Partner RFT as well as future procurement processes.
The Contributing Partner RFI:
a. is separate from, does not form part of, this RFT; and
b. is governed by its own separate process. Further details on the Contributing Partner ATM can be found on AusTender.
You are invited to submit a tender in response to Request for Tender (RFT) 13016 to provide research leadership and management services for the Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre (OET DRC).
Defence Innovation, Science and Technology Strategy 2026 (DISTS 26) calls for Defence to progress the formation of DRCs in partnership with universities and industry to focus on enduring and complex IS&T priorities that require interdisciplinary teams.
The OET DRC is a response to a fundamental shift in the role of energy within Defence capability and operations. It is intended to provide Defence with a scalable and enduring mechanism to shape the Defence energy landscape and deliver operationally relevant, deployable energy solutions that support the future Integrated Force
The OET DRC will operate as a problem-led, outcome-focused enterprise, integrating Defence, academia, industry and international partners into a coherent, mission-driven effort. Its role is not to conduct isolated, exploratory or basic research, but to accelerate the adoption, integration, and transition of energy technologies into deployable Defence capability, particularly where conventional market or program mechanisms are insufficient.

title: Private Hospital Services
description:
DVA is seeking the provision of Private Hospital services for Entitled Persons by publishing this Invitation to Provide Private Hospital Services to the Veteran Community.
DVA serves Australia’s veteran community, through the provision of programmes of care, compensation and commemoration.
DVA’s aim is to secure high quality private hospital care for Entitled Persons delivered for a fair price, at the most convenient locations for Entitled Persons. As the veteran community ages, their capacity to access a wider range of care appropriate to their needs is increasingly important. Managing emerging and different needs of contemporary veterans is also a priority. DVA also aims to continually improve the quality and safety of services, and the health outcomes for DVA clients, through the purchase of evidence-based treatment services.
DVA’s New Approach to Contracting for Private Hospital Services
In the past DVA contracted with Private Hospitals for services to Entitled Persons through a Request for Tenders (RFT).
The current process that DVA is engaging in with Private Hospital providers is not an RFT.
DVA has introduced new arrangements for providers to contract with DVA. This is a simplified contracting model that DVA is using to facilitate engagement with suitably qualified providers.
A summary of the key features of the new arrangements are:
maximising the numbers of participating providers to achieve wide access to private hospitals services for the veteran community;
there is no competition, all qualified providers can participate;
while providers are required to submit the fee tables, there is no requirement for tender submission or evaluation of tenders;
providers self-certify their compliance with DVA’s terms and conditions of the Hospital Services Agreement;
providers can enter into the Hospital Services Agreement at any time and the Hospital Services Agreement will continue until DVA ends the arrangements or the Contracting Entity exits the arrangements with DVA; and
negotiation only on fees to ensure value for money.

title: Operational Energy Transitions Defence Research Centre Contributing Partner RFI
description:
The OET DRC is being developed in response to a fundamental shift in the role of energy within Defence capability and operations. Energy is no longer a background enabler, but a central determinant of operational effectiveness, underpinning operational tempo, persistence, survivability, and freedom of action in increasingly contested and degraded environments.
To support the establishment of the OET DRC and the delivery of its Inaugural Research Projects (IRPs), the Commonwealth is undertaking two separate but related processes in parallel as follows:
1. ATM ID 13016 Lead Partner Request For Tender (RFT) (separate process): to engage a supplier as a Lead Partner to provide research leadership and expertise at the program and project level for the OET DRC; and
2. ATM ID 13457 Contributing Partner Request For Information (RFI) (this RFI): to engage with the market for the purposes of:
- understanding market capability and potential suppliers that align with, and have interest in, research related to the OET DRC Themes; and
- informing the development and conduct of other procurement processes (including future procurement processes).
This RFI is separate from the Lead Partner RFT process. Further information regarding the Lead Partner RFT can be found on AusTender under ATM ID 13016.
The OET DRC will initially address the following five areas (OET DRC Themes):
1. Dispersed Energy Access at the Tactical Edge
2. Sustainment Under Contested Conditions
3. Resilient and Scalable Forward Energy Systems
4. Enabling Next-Generation High-Power and High-Consumption Capabilities
5. Extended Endurance and Reduced Logistic Dependence
Defence’s overall objective is to support innovative, low Technology Readiness Level research that advances new knowledge, develops emerging concepts or prototypes and has the potential to contribute to future capability outcomes associated with the OET DRC Themes.
This RFI invites entities interested in the OET DRC Themes to provide a response that outlines their research expertise, capability and facilities. Respondents are also invited to put forward unique or novel research and technology approaches to enable practical solutions under the OET DRC Themes.

title: Land Distributed Tactical Power Management Challenge
description:
The Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator (ASCA) is accelerating the delivery of innovative capabilities to the Australian Defence Force by rapidly developing, testing and transitioning technologies that address Defence’s priority needs.
To support this initiative, ASCA is launching the Land Distributed Tactical Power Management Challenge, also referred to as the Power Challenge.
The Power Challenge is a collaborative initiative between Australia and the United Kingdom (UK) focused on advancing innovative solutions to meet emerging land force energy requirements.
You are invited to submit a tender in response to this Request for Tender (RFT) – ATM ID: ASCA-RFT-2026-LDTPM.
Through this RFT, ASCA is seeking tenders to develop and demonstrate innovative solutions that address one or more of the following Desired Capability Effects (DCEs):
DCE 1 – Company Level Power Generation and Management
A modular, scalable and low-signature power capability that supports dispersed company-level operations for up to 72 hours independently of higher-echelon power sources. The capability may incorporate power generation, energy storage, energy replenishment and power distribution functions, and should support operations at company, platoon and section levels.
DCE 2 – Tactical Edge Power
A modular and scalable power capability that enables platoons, sections and individual soldiers to operate for up to 48 hours without reliance on company-level replenishment capabilities. The capability may incorporate local power generation, energy storage, energy harvesting, battery exchange or energy replenishment functions suitable for operation at the tactical edge. Multiple DCE 2 systems may be employed to meet platoon-level energy requirements.

title: Cyber Authorisation Process Reform solution

The key needs and requirements for the technology solution have been identified as follows:
a. Enables lifecycle management of cyber secure Defence Technology Systems from identification through retirement, independent of delivery pathway or organisational structure.
b. Enables a canonical Technology System record linking identity, ownership, scope, mission context, architecture, dependencies, composition, security controls, evidence, cyber risk, findings, exceptions, decisions and lifecycle history.

title: To establish a Contract for Procurement of Synthetic Paper Products.
description:
The Defence Print and Distribution Service (DPDS) requires the supply of synthetic paper stock to support the production of Australian Defence Force (ADF) publications and other products intended for field deployment.
Synthetic paper stock is an essential requirement for ADF field publications and other products due to its unique performance characteristics. Standard paper products cannot adequately replicate the required performance characteristics. The material provides superior durability through its waterproof, tear-resistant, and flexible properties, enabling publications/products to withstand harsh operational and environmental conditions encountered during Defence activities.
In addition to its durability, the synthetic stock must be fully compatible with DPDS production printing equipment. Compatibility is critical to maintaining high-volume production efficiency, minimising printer jams, feed issues, large build ups of paper related dust in the equipment and static-related complications, while ensuring consistent print quality and operational readiness.
DPDS requires approximately 70,000 sheets of synthetic paper stock per month to support its ongoing production requirements. DPDS is seeking to engage a suitably qualified supplier to provide synthetic paper stock under a supply arrangement that delivers reliable product availability, consistent quality, value for money and ongoing support to Defence printing operations.

title: Notice of RFT - Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel of Outreach Program Counsellors for the
description:
This is a pre-release notice to provide advance notification of a proposed RFT for the Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel.
Please note, eligibility, application requirements, assessment processes, and contractual arrangements will be set out in the forthcoming RFT. No evaluation criteria, scoring methodology, or commercial terms are being released at this stage. The Department reserves the right to modify or cancel the proposed RFT at its discretion.
Background on Open Arms
Open Arms is Australia’s national accredited provider of mental health and wellbeing services for veterans and the families of veterans.
Open Arms provides mental health counselling, relationship counselling, peer support services, and group programs for people with Australian Defence Force (ADF) service (current and former serving members) and their immediate families.
Open Arms provides free and confidential counselling through a national network of multidisciplinary mental health professionals, delivered in dedicated Open Arms centres by the DVA’s staff, or through the Panel; being a network of accredited mental health clinicians, engaged to support the delivery of services on behalf of Open Arms across Australia through the Outreach Program.
Open Arms can provide counselling, care coordination and peer support services to veterans and the families of veterans within an episode of care model, where clients engage with our services for goal directed interventions for a defined period.
Open Arms aims to provide timely access to appropriate services and care, based on a comprehensive holistic assessment and integrated care pathways to meet client needs and support recovery. This includes working in partnership with health systems, including primary health, as well as other community agencies to ensure comprehensive support for our clients.
Background on the Panel and Outreach Program
Open Arms’ Model of Care provides the organisational framework that underpins the delivery of all Outreach Program services. It guides how we support veterans and the families of veterans through trauma-informed, military-aware, recovery-oriented care, while ensuring consistent clinical governance, quality service delivery and positive client outcomes. In 2024 the Panel was established through which Outreach Providers provide Open Arms services to clients. The Panel is the mechanism for Open Arms to engage with Outreach Providers to ensure the highest level of support can be delivered to clients. Only organisations or individuals appointed to the Panel can provide Open Arms Outreach Program Counselling Services.
The categories of services that are delivered through the Panel include:
Outreach Program Counsellors (OPCs), who provide individual, couples, or family counselling
Group Program Facilitators (GPFs), who facilitate evidence-informed, military-aware group programs that strengthen resilience, build practical skills, and promote wellbeing
Clinical Supervisors, who provide professional supervision to Open Arms’ staff.
Outreach Providers on the Panel can provide one, two or all three service streams, depending on their qualifications, experience and the services they are approved to deliver.
Go to the Open Arms website for further information:
https://www.openarms.gov.au/about/open-arms-outreach-program
Expansion of definition of OPC
In 2025 the Veterans’ Entitlements (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025 and the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025), were enacted which amended the MRCA Treatment Principles (No. MRCC 53/2013) and the Treatment Principles (Instrument 2013 No. R52) – (collectively the Treatment Principles) – to expand the types of professions who can provide Outreach Program Counselling as an Outreach Program Counsellor (OPC). Now that occupational therapists, registered nurses, social workers (general) and counsellors are recognised as additional profession types eligible to apply to become a provider, the Department wishes to update the Panel accordingly through the proposed RFT.
The Department is therefore looking to procure Outreach Providers from the following eligible professions:
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a psychologist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as an occupational therapist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a registered nurse;
a person who is eligible for membership with the Australian Association of Social Workers;
or
a person who is registered:
as a registered clinical counsellor with the Psychotherapy and Counselling Federation of Australia;
as a counsellor at registration category Level 3 or Level 4 with the Australian Counselling Association Limited.
The Department is currently planning to release the RFT to market through publication on AusTender in September 2026, however this timeframe may be subject to change.
Please note that this is not an RFT and does not commit the Department to proceed. The Close Date and Time stated in this notice relates to this pre-release notice only and does not reflect the proposed RFT commencement and closing dates for potential tenderers to lodge their submissions. The RFT, where undertaken, will be published on AusTender and will include the Closing Date and Time for lodgement of submissions.

title: Navy Way Point Leadership Program
description:
Navy Training Authority Initial Training Leadership and Management (TA-ITLM) requires a suitably qualified Supplier to develop and deliver the Navy Way Point program. The program is designed to complement the current Navy Senior Leadership Program (NSLP) and other existing career professional development offerings.
In order to provide a more career-focused professional development opportunity for Captains, particularly those who are new to the Canberra environment, Navy is seeking a reality-based program with a focus on participant interaction, containing practical exercises based on real world scenarios.
The aim of the Way Point Program is to develop the ability of selected senior officers to comprehend the strategic environment and to provide influential, Joint and Whole of Australian Government (WoAG) options that support Government strategic objectives. The course should develop participants' strategic comprehension, thinking and communication skills, and the behaviours and attitudes needed to be effective as a commander or senior staff officer in a Joint, Defence and WoAG team.
The program should include a broad range of highly experienced presenters from across the national security spectrum, with the intent to provide officers new to the Canberra environment, with the skills and confidence operating with influence in Joint, Defence, WoAG and international environments.
Each Navy Way Point program shall be five (5) days in length for up to 24 participants. Taking place in Canberra once per calendar year, with delivery in Q2 (April-June).

vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription:
The Council is committed to leading our City, protecting our environment, caring for our people, making our City vibrant, liveable, healthy and accessible, and economically and financially sustainable.
The Blue Mountains is one of only two cities in the world surrounded by a World Heritage Area and sits within the Sydney drinking water catchment servicing 1.7 million people.
vendorPanelDetails.queryCutoffAtRaw: Friday 09 October 2026 02:00 PM (AUS Eastern Daylight Time)
vendorPanelDetails.background:
Council is planning to introduce a Food and Garden Organics (FOGO) collection service for all residents in July 2027. New contracts for all three services are scheduled to commence at the start date of Council’s new FOGO service on 1 July 2027.

The new FOGO processing contract has been awarded to ANL, with FOGO to be processed at their Blayney facility. The new kerbside collection contract has been awarded to JJ’s Waste & Recycling and involves delivering FOGO to the Katoomba Waste Management Facility (KWMF) where it will be temporarily stored in the transfer station building before being loaded into trucks by Council staff for bulk transport to ANL’s Blayney facility. This procurement is for this bulk transport of FOGO from KWMF to ANL Blayney.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes:
Transporting FOGO to ANL Blayney will enable this material to be converted into compost to enrich soil for gardens and crops, rather than being wasted in landfill where it would generate greenhouse gases and leachate.

Facilitate the diversion of FOGO from landfill, this procurement will ensure the continuing contribution to the following two Progress Measures specifically:

•	Decrease total waste going to landfill per capita.

•	Increase proportion of waste diverted from landfill.

publicQuestions.question:

On page 8 of the “Technical Specification C: Reporting, GIS & Deliverables” it states: “Check every property, by running water into yard gullies, to confirm how many live junctions join with the main”, however Tender Schedule 2 “Schedule of Prices” does not include a rate for this work. a.	Does Council require all tenderers to allow “Check every property, by running water into yard gullies, to confirm how many live junctions join with the main” in their tender price?

b.	If so, in which Item No. in Tender Schedule 2 “Schedule of Prices” are all tenderers to allow for this work?

a.	The Unit Rate in Item 3.8 is “Per Hour”. Is this a typographic error? Should the Unit Rate be “Per Metre?

b.	What is meant by Condition Assessment rating 0, 4 and 5? Do you require any work on Condition Assessment 1, 2 or 3? If so, please specify what is required?

4.	On page 3 of the “Technical Specification A: Pipe Cleaning, Root Cutting and CCTV” it states: “All extracted sludge, liquid waste, and solid debris must be transported and disposed of lawfully at Gundagai Transfer Station...” Arising from this we have these questions:

a.	Can Council confirm that the Gundagai Transfer Station will accept sludge, liquid waste, and solid debris removed from the sewer mains in this Contract? In our experience, some Council operated Waste Transfer Stations will not accept sludge, liquid waste, and solid debris removed from sewer mains.

b.	Is there a charge to dispose of sludge, liquid waste, and solid debris removed from the sewer mains at Gundagai Waste Transfer Station? Is so, what is the charge?

c.	Can Council specify the volume and type of material each tenderer must allow to remove from each sewer main in their tender price, to ensure Council can compare “apples with apples” when assessing tenders?

publicQuestions.question: Could Council possibly provide pipe diameter and pipe material information, as this information does not appear to be included in the tender documents?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

All sewer mains currently identified within the scope of the Contract are DN150. Based on Council's available asset information, the sewer mains included within the cleaning, root cutting and CCTV scope comprise Vitrified Clay (VC), concrete and PVC pipes. Asbestos Cement (AC) sewer mains are excluded from cleaning and root-cutting activities under this Contract.

Tenderers should note that Council's existing asset information may not necessarily represent the actual condition or material of every asset in the field. publicQuestions.question:
Could Council please clarify the intended methodology for cleaning, CCTV inspection and root cutting?

The specification states that pipelines must be cleaned prior to CCTV inspection and that root cutting in asbestos cement sewer mains is prohibited. As pipe material and the presence of roots would need to be identified prior to undertaking root cutting, our understanding is that CCTV inspection may be required following cleaning to identify root intrusions and determine whether root cutting is appropriate.

We also note that the ITP references "Post-Cut CCTV Verification" for mechanical root cutting. If Council requires CCTV inspection both prior to and following root cutting, this would result in some sections being CCTV inspected twice. The tender schedule does not appear to differentiate or allow for multiple CCTV inspections of the same sewer main length.

Could Council please confirm the intended methodology and whether the nominated CCTV quantity is intended to include any CCTV verification required following root cutting?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

The specifications states that pipelines must be cleaned prior to CCTV inspection and that root cutting is asbestos, cement sewer mains is prohibited. As pipe material and the presence of roots would need to be identified prior to undertaking root cutting, our understanding is that CCTV inspection may be required following cleaning to identify root intrusions and determine whether root cutting is appropriate.

We also note that ITP reference “Post – Cut CCTV verification” for mechanical root cutting. If Council requires CCTV inspection both prior to and following root cutting, this would result in some sections being CCTV inspected twice. The tender schedule does not appear to differentiate or allow for multiple CCTV inspections of the same sewer main length.

Council does not intend to prescribe a specific methodology or sequence for undertaking the cleaning, CCTV inspection and root-cutting activities. Tenderers are expected to be suitably experienced and competent in sewer-main cleaning, CCTV inspection, condition assessment and root cutting and shall develop and submit an appropriate methodology for undertaking the Works
in accordance with the Technical Specification, applicable standards, WHS requirements and the conditions encountered in the field. The Contractor's methodology shall demonstrate how the Works will be undertaken without causing damage to Council's sewer infrastructure and shall address, as applicable, pipe material and condition, cleaning requirements, identification and removal of root intrusions, CCTV inspection, post-work verification, waste capture and disposal, flow management and protection of existing assets.

The restrictions specified in the Technical Specification, including the prohibition on root cutting of Asbestos Cement (AC) sewer mains, remain applicable. The Contractor shall satisfy itself as to the suitability of its proposed equipment and methodology for the pipe material, condition and circumstances encountered during the Works. Where conditions are encountered that prevent the Works from being safely or satisfactorily undertaken in accordance with the Technical Specification, the Contractor shall notify the Principal Authorised Person (PAP) and obtain direction before proceeding.

CCTV Inspection and Post-Work Verification

The CCTV quantity included in Tender Schedule 2 represents the nominated sewer-main length for CCTV inspection and condition assessment. Where cleaning and/or root cutting requires additional CCTV viewing or verification to demonstrate that the work has been satisfactorily completed, tenderers shall allow for such verification within their tendered cleaning/root-cutting rates. Such verification will not constitute a separate full CCTV inspection for payment purposes.

Where the PAP specifically directs an additional full CCTV inspection or condition assessment outside the nominated scope, the additional work will be valued using the applicable rates in Tender Schedule 2. Tenderers shall make their own assessment of the methodology, sequencing, plant, equipment and resources necessary to achieve the specified outcomes when preparing their Tender.

Kind regards

CGRC

publicQuestions.question: Are there hydrants available within Gundagai that can be used for water filling?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

Council's reticulated water network includes hydrants within Gundagai; however, the Contractor shall not draw water directly from a Council hydrant. The Contractor shall use only a nominated water filling point for water required for sewer-main cleaning and jetting.

publicQuestions.answer:

The approved filling point is located in William Street, Gundagai (near cemetery).

Kind regards

CGRC

publicQuestions.question: Can Council provide any applicable water usage charges or fees?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

No usage charges will be applicable however access to water from the mains will be restricted to jetting and cleaning of sewer mains only.

Kind regards

CGRC

title: Short-Term Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country
description:
Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country (Short-Term) - WS5659204351

The Coordinator of Energy has determined, under clause 3.11A.4 of the Electricity System Market (ESM) Rules, to trigger a Non-Co-optimised Essential System Services (NCESS) procurement process by Western Power for Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country.

The proposed services aim to address reliability and system strength concerns during planned or unplanned outage events affecting one or more 132 kV transmission lines supplying the North Country.

Call for NCESS Submissions

Western Power invites NCESS Submissions from prospective NCESS providers to deliver Reliability Services and/or System Strength Services located in the North Country. The North Country is defined as the area supplied by the Rangeway, Geraldton and Chapman substations.

This tender relates to the Short-Term contract term option (1-4 year terms). Proponents may offer a solution that fully or partially meets the requirements for either service (or both).

Activation requirements, performance measures, preferred connection locations and other technical requirements are set out in the Final NCESS Service Specification.

Queries may be submitted by email to emerging.technology.portfolio@westernpower.com.au or via the Q&A function in the VendorPanel portal.

Please submit NCESS Submissions via VendorPanel no later than 5:00pm (AWST) on 12 October 2026.

Interested NCESS providers should register with VendorPanel to be informed of whether any supporting documentation such as clarifications to questions may be published.

title: Call for Expressions of Interest: System Restart Service (SWIS-wide)
description:
AEMO is seeking Expressions of Interest (EOI) to understand the availability, location and readiness of Facilities that may be able to provide System Restart Service across the SWIS.

Previous System Restart Service engagements have indicated that other existing or new Facilities may also be capable of providing System Restart Service, subject to necessary site works, testing and lead times.

AEMO invites Market Participants, or prospective Market Participants, with Facilities capable of providing System Restart Service to make submissions for:

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence from 23 October 2028 (EOI Part 1); and

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence only after October 2030 (EOI Part 2).

AEMO welcomes submissions for either existing or proposed Facilities with different technology configurations to submit an EOI. The EOI will be used by AEMO to determine the requirements of a subsequent tender, such as the location of the service (Sub-Network) and service commencement period.

AEMO will specifically use the information from the EOI to:

* identify a short-list of candidates that are able to meet the System Restart Standard;

* assess the efficacy to provide System Restart Services;

* review and potentially amend the System Restart Standard, including the Electrical Sub-Network boundaries (i.e. this is to determine the location AEMO will be tendering for the System Restart Service); and

* confirm with short-listed candidates any necessary upgrades or capital works to be compliant with the future System Restart Standard and the System Restart Service Specification and identify associated timelines to provide the service.

All submissions:

* must be provided in good faith but are not binding on the respondent; and

* will be treated as confidential information under applicable Electricity System and Market Rules.

Submissions must be provided via VendorPanel in accordance with the EOI Guideline by 5pm AWST on 9 November 2026.

The Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service own and operate a range of Generators and Diesel Generator Power Plant Equipment that provide emergency power supply to facilities and infrastructure. Maintenance is required to optimise their performance over the life of the equipment to ensure security of power supply.

Objectives:

(i)	Preventative maintenance

vendorPanelDetails.background:
Preventative Maintenance

Queensland Health and Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service seek to engage Supplier(s) capable of providing all elements of Generator Servicing & Diesel Tank Inspections. Preventative maintenance is to be undertaken in a planned, timely and cost-effective manner with the objective being to maximise reliability, minimise equipment downtime and repairs and reduce costs to Queensland Health and taxpayers.

To ensure emergency supplies of electricity is maintained for all Queensland Health facilities, Generators and Diesel Generator Power Plant equipment are required to perform at optimal levels for safety, technical, operations and environmental considerations. All Generators and Diesel Generator Power Plant equipment are required to adhere to legislative requirements, Australian Standards, Queensland Health Task Specifications and Manufacturer Recommendations.

Corrective Maintenance

Queensland Health and Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service seek to engage Supplier(s) capable of providing all elements Generator and Diesel Generator Power Plant corrective maintenance or part thereof.

Corrective maintenance is to be undertaken in a timely and cost-effective manner to ensure Queensland Health and Torres and Cape Hospital and Health Service maintain uninterrupted use of Generator and Diesel Generator Power Plant in order to meet operational requirements.

To ensure emergency supplies of electricity is maintained for all Queensland Health facilities, Generators and Diesel Generator Power Plant equipment are required to be repaired to a standard that allows equipment to perform at optimal levels for safety, technical, operations and environmental considerations. All repairs and corrective maintenance are to ensure Generators and Diesel Generator Power Plant equipment adhere to legislative requirements, Australian Standards, Queensland Health Task Specifications and Manufacturer Recommendations.

title: New Reservoir at Bamaga
description:
Northern Peninsular Area Council is looking to expand the amount of storage available at their Bamaga Reservoir site.

At present there are 2 x 1.6ML concrete tanks that receive water via the Clear Water Pump Station at our Water Treatment Plant.

We would like to increase supply by at least another 1.6ML in size.

The top water level would need to be the same as the existing reservoirs.

This will be a design/ construct project, with the design needing to be approved by Council before proceeding to the construction phase.

We are expecting the design and planning work to happen during the upcoming wet season, with construction starting in May/ June 2027.

Level Sensors and Outlet Flow Meter will be provided as part of this contract. Council will ensure these are integrated into our SCADA system.

The design, construction and commissioning of the reservoir will be in accordance with the Unity Water Specification Pr9821.

The location of the site is Lot 107 on SP284242. Latitude: -10.899929, Longitude: 142.38935.

Council will provide a laydown area close to the construction site for storage of materials. There is limited internal storage for sensitive items so containers may be considered to keep some items out of the weather.

Council can provide a donga as a site office. There is power to the site that can be utilised. Council can also provide some portable toilets for the site.

Council will provide accommodation for the duration of the project.

There is limited plant and equipment available for hire for this project, but there may be opportunity for short term hire of items such as tippers, excavators, skid steers and s grader. Council does not own a crane or a manitou.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes:

At present we the daily usage across the NPA is around 5.5ML/day but we only have 3.2ML of storage at Bamaga which supplies the whole area. There are a further 4 x 1.6ML tanks at Umagico, Injinoo, New Mapoon and Seisia, which are all gravity fed from Bamaga.

Tenders will be assessed on Price, Guaranteed serviceable life of the structure, experience in construction work in remote locations, employment and or training opportunities for local people.

publicQuestions.question:
Hello and greetings!

We would like to request for the tender booklet documents stating all the requirements for the tender submission of the project, response schedules, mandatory and non-mandatory criteria, and other commercial requirements, apart from the technical specifications and layout already provided in the portal. Kindly advise. Thank you!

Warm regards,
publicQuestions.answer:
Unfortunately NPARC does not have a team of Engineers that can supply all the information that you are seeking.

That's why this has gone out as a Design, Construct Tender.

The contract will be based on AS4000:2025.

publicQuestions.question:
General Comment

•	Only the general Reservoir Design Specification has been provided; we are missing the document containing the Project Specific Requirements for Bamaga.

•	The Specification does not appear to include tailoring to the Bamaga-specific/NPA context.

3.0 Planning Information

1.	Site RP description and site location.

2.	Land tenure is assumed to be DOGIT, despite the Specification requiring land to be Unity Water owned (Sect 3.2).

3.	Survey data, including levels.

4.	Preliminary site geotechnical information.

5.	Reservoir operating parameters to AHD (e.g. BWL, MOL, Overflow Level).

6.	Available planning or engineering reporting.

7.	Treated water quality information prior to detailed design.

8.	Minimum HGL at the interconnection points for HL and sizing of interconnecting pipework.

9.	Current status of power supply to site.

10.	Access road requirements – minimum 4 m width, chainage and extent.

If any of the above information cannot be provided to a satisfactory level of detail, it should form the basis of a scope clarification.

4.0 General Design

•	Stakeholder requirements – clarify whether Unity Water/NPARC are responsible for stakeholder negotiations.

•	Landscaping – confirm whether this is required in the NPA context.

•	Precast concrete columns – confirm acceptability.

•	Galvanised steel beams based on Draper Road – confirm acceptability.

•	To allow for minimisation of columns as requested, confirm purlins and aluminium roof sheeting as per Specification can be adopted to achieve the specified 50-year design life.

10.0 Water Quality

In the absence of treated water quality information, there is no confirmed requirement for pH correction or supplemental chlorine dosing. Water treatment/dosing is therefore not included in the tender but could be provided, if required, as a cost variation.

1.	CFD modelling – confirm whether required by the Client to determine the reservoir mixing rate in accordance with Appendix D. Approximate cost $50,000.

2.	Passive mixing (preferred option) may be provided with an inlet nozzle, should a low-level inlet be acceptable for water transfer requirements.

3.	Consider provision of a 100 mm suction and discharge point in the reservoir wall and space for future recirculation pumping and Cl dosing.

4.	Water quality testing will not be available in NPA; sampling, preservation and transport to Cairns, including associated costs, will need to be considered.

12.0 Electrical

•	Confirm whether power augmentation is required and, if so, the location of the upgrade connection point.

•	Suggest excluding power supply augmentation until the scope is known.

•	Requirements for integration with existing NPARC SCADA have not been identified.

•	Unity Water-approved supplier requirements may be an issue in NPA (e.g. Sect 12.5 Radio Path Survey).

Mandatory Meeting

•	Confirm mandatory meeting requirements, including timing and required attendees.
publicQuestions.answer:
G1 and G2: NPARC does not have an Engineering Team that can provide local specifications for jobs such as this. I picked the Unity Water Specifications because they were the best ones that were freely available. We will adjust these to suit the Bamaga requirements.

P1: The site is located on Lot 107 on SP284242. Latitude: -10.899929, Longitude: 142.38935

P2: The land is administered by NPARC under DOGIT Legislation.

P3: I have included the latest survey data that I have for that site in the files area. I cannot locate a contours survey for the site. That will have to be included in the design planning phase.

P4: There has been no geotechnical tests conducted at the site. That will need to be included in the design investigations as well.

P5: These have been provided in the text.

P6: There are no planning or engineering reports for this site.

P7: Water Quality results from the drinking water quality management plan have been added to the files.

P8: Pipe sizes should be matched to the existing pipework - 150mm inlet and 250mm outlet and overflow.

P9: There is sufficient power to the site.

P10: There is a steep but adequate access road to the site. NPARC will maintain the road to ensure that it is accessible for trucks and machinery to access the site.

G1: NPARC will be responsible for all Stakeholder requirements.

G2: There are no specific landscaping requirements. The site is to be left clean, level and accessible for plant and vehicles.

G3: Precast concrete columns are acceptable.

G4: Galvanised beams would not be preferred because of the salt air in this region.

G5: Purlins and aluminium roof sheeting will be allowed.

W1: CFD Modelling will not be required.

W2: Passive mixing is preferred.

W3: There is no requirement for 100 mm suction and discharge points.

W4: Veolia will be able to assist with water quality testing. They have an on-site lab and conduct their own tests at the WTP.

E1: There will Be no requirement for power augmentation.

E2: Excluded.

E3: Integration with SCADA is excluded. Contractor will have to assist our SCADA Techs with access to level sensors, valves, instruments, etc.

E4: Ignore the Unity Water approved supplier requirements.

M1: There will be no Mandatory Meeting. It is too hard to get everyone up to Bamaga, especially at this time of the year. I prefer to use Vendor Panel for communication.

publicQuestions.question:
Based on the Unity Water specification the it appears as though the top storage level is only 60% of the capacity, therefore the total volume of the tank should be 2.24ML, is this correct?

It also suggests that the top water level should be the same as the existing, what is this level?
publicQuestions.answer:
(edited on 25/Sep/2026 02:41 PM)

The top water level of the current reservoirs is 77.12mAHD and the bottom water level is 73.68mAHD.

I was unaware of the 60% of capacity requirement in the Unity Water specifications. I will discuss this with them and get back to you.

I have reviewed this requirement and will allow a top water level of 80% because all feed to the tanks is controlled by the high lift pumps.

The AHD levels given above must be maintained.

publicQuestions.question: We have formwork to allow us to construct an effective capacity of 1.561ML based on the RLs provided, will this be acceptable?
publicQuestions.answer: Yes, we will accept that size.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi,

Could you please provide clarification on the following items regarding the proposed Bamaga Reservoir works:

1. Could Council please confirm whether a Stainless Steel (SS) reservoir would be acceptable as an alternative reservoir construction material, subject to meeting the specified capacity, design life and applicable technical requirements?

2. Could Council please confirm whether the concrete required for construction of the reservoir and associated works will be supplied by Council?

Your clarification would be greatly appreciated.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Yes, a stainless steel reservoir would be acceptable to Council.

2. Yes, Council will supply the concrete for this project. In your responses, please indicate the volume and strength requirements for concrete and your rate for laying the concrete. All reinforcing and formwork materials must be supplied by the contractor.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi,

With reference to the Unitywater specifications, the links provided within the specification are currently inaccessible. Could Council please provide the applicable referenced Unitywater specifications/documents or updated accessible links?
publicQuestions.answer: Can you please clarify which links you are trying to access.

publicQuestions.question:
Can Council please confirm whether the head contractor is required to hold a QBCC licence for this contract, and if so, the licence class and financial category Council expects?

Our understanding is that construction of a water supply reservoir and its connections to the existing mains may fall under Schedule 1, s11 of the QBCC Regulation 2018 (work for water reticulation systems) and therefore not constitute building work. We’d appreciate Council’s position on this, including whether a QBCC licence is a contract requirement regardless of the statutory position.
publicQuestions.answer: You are correct, construction of the reservoir and connects to the existing main, does not require a QBCC Licence.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi,

Could Council please consider granting a two-week extension to the tender submission deadline for the Bamaga Reservoir Project?

We would appreciate your consideration and look forward to your response.
publicQuestions.answer:
This tender has been open since 16th September and some respondents have already submitted their tenders.

Therefore I will not be able to extend the closing date.

publicQuestions.question:
To allow the scope to be priced correctly, could you please confirm the following:

1. Chemical dosing

Is chemical dosing (e.g. chlorine boosting or pH correction) at the new reservoir part of the contract scope? If so, please advise the chemical type and dosing point, and whether a dosing shed, chemical storage and dosing equipment are to be supplied.

2. Site security and temporary fencing

Are there any known security concerns at the reservoir site? Is temporary fencing required around the works area for the duration of construction?

3. Electrical works

Are there any electrical works in the contract? If so, please describe what they include.

4. Flowmeter and flowmeter pit

Please confirm that the flowmeter and flowmeter pit will be supplied by Council.

5. Wiring and switchboard

Will all wiring and the electrical switchboard be completed by Council, or should these be included in the tender price? If they are to be included, please provide any switchboard requirements or Council standards to be allowed for.

We note from the earlier Q&A that the existing power supply is sufficient and SCADA integration is excluded. These questions are to confirm where the boundary sits between Council's electrical scope and the contractor's.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. There is no requirement for Chemical Dosing or dosing points for this reservoir.

2. There is no security concerns at the site. I would advise placing temp fencing or gates to the access roads up to the site designating the site as a construction zone and restricting access to the site. Veolia have to access the site for maintenance of the other two reservoirs and to take water samples, so you will need to delineate the construction zone in some form.

3. There is no requirement for electrical or SCADA works for this contract, other than assisting our contractors to access the site when required.

4. There is no requirement for a flow meter or pit.

5. All wiring and switchboard work will be carried out by a separate contractor.

vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription:
** ABOUT THE BEGA VALLEY **

The Bega Valley Shire is located at the south-eastern corner of New South Wales, halfway between Australia’s two largest cities, Sydney and Melbourne and three hours’ drive from the nation’s capital, Canberra.

Our coastal fringe extends from Wallaga Lake in the north to Cape Howe and the Victorian border in the south. Collectively this 225-kilometre section forms the beautiful Sapphire Coast, the heart of Australia’s Coastal Wilderness.

Our community vision explains our collective aspiration that we are an inclusive and welcoming community that integrates quality of life, prosperity, sustainable development and conservation of the environment. Our connection to Country is guided by the culture and heritage of our Traditional Owners.

** ABOUT COUNCIL **

Bega Valley Shire Council is responsible for providing all of the typical local government services across the Bega Valley Shire including maintaining a broad range of assets valued at over $1.7 billion that allow our visitors and community alike to live, work and play.

The Bega Valley Shire is governed by an elected Council comprising nine Councillors. Councillors provide leadership and establish policy and strategic direction for the organisation and the future of the shire.

Delivering the day to day services for council is a professional and dynamic staff cohort of over 560 people including full time, contract and casual positions.

Contractors to council play an important and valued role, assisting us delivering services and projects to the highest of standards and value for money.

** WHAT COUNCIL DOES **

Provide and maintain community facilities such as:
•	Parks and sportsgrounds
•	Playgrounds and skate parks
•	Sapphire Aquatic centre Pambula and swimming pools throughout the shire
•	Sports and recreation facilities throughout the Shire
•	Local libraries in Bega, Bermagui, Eden and Merimbula
•	Preschools and Childcare centres in Bega and Eden, and our Mobile service for Candelo and Bemboka
•	Merimbula Airport, Bega Saleyards and Cemeteries throughout the Shire

We care for the environment by:
•	Managing and enhancing bushland areas
•	Providing environmental and waste education and recycling services
•	Responding to pollution incidents and prosecuting polluters
•	Monitoring the water quality of the Shire’s estuaries
•	Planting trees and controlling noxious weeds
•	Beneficially recycling and reusing treated effluent

We create a safer place to live by:
•	Maintaining and improving roads, footpaths and stormwater drains
•	Working with emergency organisations such as the Rural Fire Service, State Emergency Service, NSW Police and NSW Surf Life Saving
•	Managing the keeping of companion animals
•	Inspecting food premises
•	Treating and supplying drinking water to our community
•	Treating sewage to a high standard to protect human health

We enhance our community by:
•	Listening to community views
•	Holding citizenship ceremonies, Australia Day Celebrations and the Seniors week luncheon known as the Golden Gig
•	Offering services for seniors, young people, new migrants and people with a disability
•	Providing grants to community organisations
•	Supporting local community groups such as sporting clubs, arts, migrant groups and charities
•	Encouraging and promoting volunteering in our communities

We plan for the future by:
•	Planning and managing the urban environment
•	Preserving heritage sites
•	Consulting with the community about its needs
•	Developing long term strategic plans for Council and the Shire

title: Water Main Renewal - Little Motleys Bridge HDD - Rodeo Drive, Bowraville NSW
description:
Nambucca Valley Council is seeking suitably qualified & experienced tenderers for the Design & Construction of a water main renewal associated with the Little Motleys Bridge Replacement. The Contractor is responsible for the design development and installation of a replacement Trunk Main using HDD techniques as well as inter-connection works at both ends. Integration with the Principals concept design and coordination of Engineering design disciples.

The works included in the Contract comprise the provision of all that is necessary for the complete and proper construction, testing and commissioning of the following, in strict accordance with this Specification, the accompanying Drawings and such other drawings and standards as may be issued from time to time during the progress of the works.

The scope of works includes, but is not limited to the following:

•	Develop concept designs to enable an effective HDD installation beneath Bowra Creek.

•	Supply, construct and commission a water trunk main and all associated connections, valves and fittings.

•	Design and construct interconnections at each end of the main including one isolation valve at each end. Valves to be 450 diameter geared valves with Clockwise Closing convention.

•	Supply, construct and commission of a water trunk main high level scour pit near the eastern connection.

•	Reinstatement of existing surfaces where affected by construction activities.

•	Carry out earthworks as required to provide adequate drainage at each site post construction.

•	Documentation of the works, and

•	All other civil works necessary for satisfactory operation of the water network.

The scope of works is outlined in Attachment 1 Technical Speciation Document

A Geotechnical Assessment would form a component of Contractor Design Development if the contractor chooses to do so.

Geotechnical information (Boreholes 1 & 2) has been captured on the concept plan provided as Attachment 1 and discussed through the commentary in Attachment 3
