publicQuestions.question:
Hello,

In relation to the Street Lighting for the wombat crossing the street lighting plans in the tender docs are preliminary only and not IFC has an approved point of supply been provided for the street light?Additionally could you please confirm that the light will be a DTP type metered street light scheme as per the DTP Standard drawings in the Tender, and not a distribution Vesi Scheme street light? Would Solar Street Lighting be considered ?

Thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
The preliminary lighting design in the tender docs are for the tenderer to price the required cost for conduit trenching, pit installation, pole foundation, and pole standing. The expected standards to be adhered is VESI standard scheme as the new lighting will be handed over to Powercor. The attached DTP standard drawings are only to serve as a technical reference in construction.

The electrical design is currently being undertaken by Powercor, and the point of supply will be from the existing pole as indicated in the preliminary lighting plan. Powercor is contracted separately for electrical design, conduit placement, wiring connection, and lighting bracket installations for this project.

Lastly, solar street lighting is not included in project scope, thus will not be considered.

publicQuestions.question:
Subject: Powercor engagement and program – third-party risk

The 30 September response and the 1 October update advise that Powercor has been contracted separately for the electrical design, conduit placement, wiring and lighting bracket installation. Lighting items 5.2–5.5 are now provisional. To understand the program risk from this third-party interface, please confirm:

1. Has Powercor been formally engaged, and is the electrical design complete or still underway?

2. Has Powercor been given Council's intended construction program? Tenderers are assuming site works in November–December 2026, with Practical Completion before the Christmas shutdown.

3. Has Powercor committed to completing its design, works and connection within that program? If not, what timeframe has it given?

4. If Powercor's design, works or approvals are delayed, will the Contractor be entitled to an extension of time? And can Practical Completion be certified for the civil works if the light connection is still outstanding?

5. Will Council or the Contractor be responsible for coordinating Powercor's site access, and its work under the Contractor's traffic management?
publicQuestions.answer:
1.	Powercor has been formally engaged, and the electrical design is complete.

2.	Powercor has been informed the intended construction timeframe that is Early November – Early December 2026.

3.	Powercor is ready for site works which the contractor will be coordinating alongside Powercor contractors.

4.	Electrical plans have been completed by Powercor. And the civil contractor will receive Practical Completion Certificate if lighting connection is still outstanding.

5.	The civil contractor will be responsible for coordinating Powercor's site access, and its work under the Contractor's traffic management. This will allow the site to be operated under a single Traffic Management.

publicQuestions.question:
Documentation clarification questions:

1. SM1 kerb width - The drawings show a 300 mm SM1 kerb with no channel, but pricing item 4.3 says "600 mm SM1 kerb and channel". This changes your kerb and crushed-rock (CTCR) pricing.

2. Item 6.1 and 6.2 units. It's in m³ but covers crushed rock plus three asphalt layers. Is that the whole pavement volume (10.1 m³) or just the asphalt (5.6 m³), or is it meant to be m2?

3. Platform wearing course type - the drawing says Type H asphalt, but pricing item 6.5 says Type V.

4. Laydown area. Will Council approve one nearby on Council-managed land if suitable?
publicQuestions.answer:
1.	Correction in item 4.3, SM1 is kerb only with no channel.

2.	Please see the updated revision D detail design for quoting.

In Item 6.1, 600mm width offset from lip of kerb to pavement shall be filled with 3 layers of asphalt with existing pavement layer as bedding.

In Item 6.2, the existing pavement will only be milled and lifted with Type V asphalt to design levels.

Both item 6.1 and 6.2 can be unit M2.

3.	Correction: Raised platform wearing course will be type H as indicated in detail design (Rev D).

4.	The location for laydown area will be further discussed and confirmed in pre-construction meeting.

Please refer to addendum which is to be issued addressing the above items.

publicQuestions.question:
1. Kerb subbase (Rev D Sheet 7): The K&C laying detail shows 150 mm Class 3 FCR subbase under the kerb, but pricing item 4.1 still says 200 mm 3% CTCR. Which applies?

2. Drainage pipe depth (Rev D Sheet 20): The drawing says "drainage pipe depth to be confirmed subject to Powercor requirements". Will any change after award be a variation?

3. Full road closure: Will Council accept a full closure of Market Street between Harmony Way and High Street for most of the works, with a signed detour via Victoria Road (Harmony Way – Victoria Road – High Street), given the 10-minute maximum traffic delay in General Specification cl. 2.2.9?

4. Unattended closure: Is an unattended closure acceptable (Type 3 barriers and ROAD CLOSED / DETOUR signs to AS 1742.3, no traffic controllers at the closure points), with CFA and emergency services advised of the detour? Are there any properties needing access through the closed section?

5. Detour approval at award: Can Council approve the detour route and VMS locations at award, so the 2-week notice can start on 29 October and site works on 12 November?

6. Bus 3 turnaround: Mount Alexander Bus 3 terminates at the Market St/Harmony Way stop and appears to turn around at the Harmony Way / Market Street junction (western end of the proposed closure). Can Council confirm the bus turnaround arrangement, and whether Council or the contractor liaises with the bus operator / DTP during the closure?

7. Delayed road markings: Rev D note 79 requires thermoplastic, and Tech Spec cl. 10.3.2(b) requires the second treatment 2–4 weeks after the first. New asphalt needs to cure before the permanent marking materials are applied. The contractor proposes first-coat / temporary paint markings straight after the asphalt (7–8 Dec) so the road reopens. The permanent markings would follow on 29–30 Dec (about 25 days after asphalt): thermoplastic line and road markings, the yellow calcined bauxite coloured pavement on the crossing (resin-bound, so it needs the new asphalt to cure / age before application for the resin to bond), any cold-applied plastic or second-coat paint markings, and RRPMs.

(a) Can Practical Completion be certified on 23 Dec with the first-coat paint markings in place and these delayed markings as an outstanding item?

(b) Is a marking visit on 29–30 Dec acceptable during the Christmas period, or would Council prefer early January?

(c) Will Council accept a delay beyond 4 weeks after the first coat if the marking contractor recommends a longer cure for the resin or thermoplastic?

8. Kerb infill asphalt (Rev D Sheet 7): Pavement reinstatement adjacent to kerb shows a 75 mm base course and 75 mm intermediate course of 10 mm nominal size Type V asphalt. A 10 mm mix cannot be placed and compacted to density in a single 75 mm layer (a 10 mm mix is limited to about 50 mm per layer). To suit DTP Section 407, can Council approve Type SI asphalt for the base and intermediate courses, 20 mm nominal size, in the two 75 mm layers, with the 10 mm Type V wearing course unchanged? Type SI is Section 407's structural intermediate mix, is stiffer and more rut-resistant, costs less, and matches the 20 mm regulation course already specified under the raised platform.
publicQuestions.answer:
1.	The 150mm Class 3 FCR subbase under the kerb will apply.

2.	Except from any change in drainage pipe material, size, crown depth and length, the council will not be considering any variation for drainage after award. To clarify, the proposed drainage pipe is required to be outside of minimum clearance of new electrical conduits.

3.	Full road closure will only be accepted if the contractor can adhere strictly to proposed timeline without incurring any delays (except unfavourable weather conditions). The full closure will also demand for short construction time (suggestion of 10 business days). Please provide detailed timeline and reasoning if more than 10 business days is required for construction.

4.	Unattended closure is acceptable if the conditions from in No.3 is strictly adhered. Notice letters have been sent to nearby residents, businesses, and emergency services for the upcoming construction. The contractor still needs to send out notice letters indicating the timeframe of road closure.

5.	The tenderer needs to include the TMP, TGS and detour map, VMS locations and indicative road closure timeline in the submission for the council to review prior to award. They will be accepted at award if traffic management standards are followed.

6.	The council will take responsibility for liaising with PTV / DTP during road closure. However, the contractor will need ensure the closure setup will have minimal to no impact to bus turning movement and vehicle movement (excluding turning movement into Market St) on Harmony Way during closure.

7.	(a) Yes, Practical Completion can be certified with the first-coat paint markings in place with delayed markings as an outstanding item.

(b) The council has no problem with a marking visit on 29-30 Dec.

(c) The council will not accept a delay no longer than 5 weeks after the coat if the marking contractor recommends a longer cure for the resin or thermoplastic.

8.	Council can approve Pavement reinstatement adjacent to kerb Type SI asphalt for the base and intermediate courses, 20 mm nominal size, in the two 75 mm layers, with the 10 mm Type V wearing course. The respective line items will need to be updated in the response table when submitting.

The council will also consider if the contractor has an alternative suggestion to design profile of pavement reinstatement adjacent to kerb.

description:
Ipswich City Council (Council) covers an area of 1,090 square kilometres with a population of approximately 190,000 people. Council is responsible for a range of services and facilities in the local area. This event was declared eligible under the Disaster Relief Funding Arrangements (DRFA), allowing recovery works to be undertaken to restore damaged road infrastructure across the LGA.

Ipswich City Council is seeking to engage a suitably experienced and qualified contractor to undertake sealed road asset restoration works across multiple sites across multiple locations.

Ipswich is centrally located in the booming south east Queensland region of Australia. To the east is the capital city Brisbane, and to the west are the rural and agricultural areas of the Brisbane, Lockyer and Fassifern Valleys. The city is ideally positioned on the national road network - 40 minutes drive from Brisbane, an hours drive from the Gold Coast and 60 minutes drive from domestic and international air and sea ports.
Ipswich comprises an area of 1090 square kms and has a population of 180,000 people. Ipswich enjoys a subtropical climate and is a safe, friendly and multicultural city. Residents come from 115 different ethnic backgrounds, speaking 84 languages.

Ipswich proudly preserves and still operates from many of its historical buildings and homes, with more than 6000 heritage-listed sites. title: Scope and Design Capella Office Air Conditioning Upgrades
description:
Central Highlands Regional Council (Council) is seeking submissions for the mechanical and electrical design, scoping and preparation of works for the replacement of the existing office air conditioning system at the Capella Council Office.

The current system experiences frequent breakdowns and is nearing the end of its operational life, resulting in escalating costs for call-outs and issues finding replacement parts. These failures also cause discomfort for both staff and customers while repairs are undertaken.

Council is seeking mechanical & electrical services for the upgrade of the AC units.

Mechanical Services?

- Detailed site investigation and verification of as-built conditions

- Remaining operational life of the existing system

- Heat load calculations for all conditioned spaces

- Selection, sizing, and design of HVAC systems (Split system unless justified otherwise)

- Decommissioning and safely dispose of the old HVAC system (if required)

- Design and assessment of outside air make-up

- Concept and Schematic (~70%) design drawings, including equipment schedules and outline specifications

- Document all necessary building works

- Existing HVAC design drawings are attached in Attachment C

This project involves the design, scoping, and preparation of work for the replacement of the existing office air conditioning system.

The works involve:?

- Installation of new air conditioning and verification of existing infrastructure?

- Concept and schematic design, documentation, and certification of mechanical and electrical systems

- Design must confirm system capacity, not just comment on existing services

- Advise, design and scope to change system to split system - including whether option is available for the use of vents in the ceiling to assist with distribution of cool air

- The project will assess the feasibility of utilising existing ductwork and vents where possible

- Where existing vents are compatible with the new split-system air conditioning units, they may be retained to minimise disruption and cost

- Any vents or ducting found to be incompatible with the new system will be removed and replaced as required to ensure optimal airflow and system performance

- The final design will confirm the number, location, and type of vents needed to achieve consistent climate control across the facility (If required)

- The intent is to provide a compliant and energy-efficient building services design suitable for Design & Construct delivery, enabling the contractor to complete detailed design and construction without major redesign

Preliminary Works

- Review existing air conditioning system documentation, drawings, and maintenance history

- Undertake site inspection/s to assess the condition of the current air conditioning system, and associated infrastructure

- Identify system requirements, load calculations, and any constraints impacting design

Design

- Prepare a design proposal for the replacement AC units, ensuring compliance with relevant Australian Standards and building codes

- Assess integration with existing Building Management Systems (BMS), electrical supply, and associated controls

- Provide design options considering energy efficiency, system reliability, and lifecycle costs

- Incorporate AC system replacement requirements within the design

Scope Documentation

- Develop a detailed Scope of Works for the AC systems replacement, including:

 - Equipment specifications (capacity, efficiency ratings, footprint)

 - Connection requirements (hydraulic, electrical, controls)

 - Demolition/removal methodology for existing

 - Installation methodology for new equipment

 - Testing and commissioning requirements

 - Warranty and maintenance obligations

Deliverables

- Report detailing the existing system and recommending the best possible solution

- Finalised design documentation

- Assessment of split-system feasibility

- Electrical capacity assessment

- Detailed Scope of Works document suitable for tendering/quoting

- Cost estimate (indicative) for replacement works

- Implementation timeline and staging recommendations to minimise disruption to office operations

Exclusions

- Actual supply, installation, or commissioning of new chiller/cassettes (covered under future works contract)

- Upgrades to unrelated mechanical, electrical, or structural systems not impacted by this replacement

Standards and Compliance

All design and documentation must comply with:

- Australian Standards AS 1668, AS/NZS 3666, AS 1851

- National Construction Code (NCC)

- Workplace Health and Safety (WHS) requirements

publicQuestions.question:
Can you please answer / confirm the following to assist in the completion of the tender response:

1. AI defect detection is core to this RFT, but cl. 6 requires 3 months' notice and consent before any AI System is used. Please confirm:

 - The AI System in the successful tender is taken to be consented to when the contract is signed.

 - The 3-month notice applies only to later changes to it (as in SR As-A-Service •10, Licensed Software •9 and Hardware •9).

If so, will Council write this consent into the Solution Requirements?

2. Does Council has a current camera or road-defect inspection provider. If it does, what data, imagery and hardware (if any) will be handed over to the successful tenderer.

3.What are the definitions (and ideally an example images) that Council or AssetAI use for the following Appendix A subtypes: Streaking, High Friction Surface Deterioration, Road Surface Failure, Sweeping and Wheel Track Cracking. Please also confirm how Bleeding and Flushing are distinguished.

Thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Council confirms that AI defect detection is a core requirement of this RFT.

The AI System proposed by the successful tenderer, as described in its tender response and incorporated into the agreed Solution Requirements, will be regarded as consented to for the purposes of the Agreement when the contract is executed. This consent is limited to the identified AI System, its agreed functions, data flows, processing purposes and operating arrangements.

The three-month notice requirement applies to subsequent upgrades, releases, enhancements or other material changes to an AI System forming part of the Solution. Where a proposed change introduces a different AI System, materially changes the processing purpose or materially changes the way Council Data is processed, Council’s prior consent will also be required under the Agreement.

Council will record the applicable consent in the final Solution Requirements and will retain its rights to require testing, security, privacy, data-protection and acceptance checks before a changed AI System is implemented.

2. Retina Visions is currently contracted for supplying the services detailed in the RFT. Under our agreement with them Council loses portal access upon contract termination. Data can be accessed by Council 14 days post contract termination, provided in CSV or GeoJSON.

3. Streaking - Longitudinal bands or lines of inconsistent binder, commonly associated with spray-seal application, that also impacts adhesion of aggregate to the pavement.

High Friction Surface Deterioration – Visible deterioration or loss of high-friction surface treatment. Typically applied to intersections or at signals where traffic breaks suddenly, aggregate polishes over time or is plucked out.

Road Surface Failure – Collects surface defect that doesn’t align with another category. A general or severe loss of the road surface’s functional integrity.

Sweeping – Collection of material, including loose aggregate, on the road surface that requires collection using a street sweeper.

Wheel Track Cracking - Cracking occurring predominantly along one or both wheel paths, generally associated with traffic loading or pavement fatigue.

Bleeding and flushing and detailed in the document https://tfnswforms.transport.nsw.gov.au/45062681-395k-seal-reseal-design-calculation-sheet.pdf

publicQuestions.question:
Council refers to AssetAI, Reflect and TechnologyOne as part of the required data pathway. Can Council confirm whether Tenderers may propose a supplier-managed platform that performs image ingestion, AI-assisted defect identification, geolocation/measurement, human review and approval, and maintains the associated evidence and audit trail, before approved defect data is exchanged with Council systems such as TechnologyOne, AssetAI and Reflect via appropriate APIs or structured data interfaces?

Additionally, does Council have any preference or requirement regarding Australian data residency, sovereign hosting, security assurance, or retention of historic imagery and inspection evidence within that platform?
publicQuestions.answer:
Council is open to Tenderers proposing a supplier-managed platform that performs image ingestion, AI-assisted defect identification, geolocation and measurement, and maintains associated evidence and audit trail information, provided the proposed solution is capable of integrating with Council's nominated systems, including TechnologyOne, AssetAI and Reflect.

Council's current operating model involves the review, validation and approval of identified defects within Council systems. Tenderers should submit proposals that support this operating model.

Council is, however, open to considering alternative approaches whereby review, validation and approval activities are undertaken within a supplier-managed platform. Where such an approach is proposed, Tenderers should clearly identify any cost, licensing, implementation, operational, performance or efficiency implications, together with the proposed governance, audit and oversight arrangements.

Council requires access to all supporting imagery, metadata, audit trail information and associated records generated throughout the inspection and defect management process. Council also has a strong preference for Australian data residency and hosting arrangements. Historic imagery and inspection evidence must remain accessible to support Council's statutory, regulatory, legal and disaster recovery obligations, including the validation of natural disaster claims.

title: Tender 10-27 Design and Construct Boardwalk Jeffery Court, Agnes Water
description:
Gladstone Regional Council (GRC) requires a suitably qualified Contractor to undertake the Design and Construct of an Australian-manufactured fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) Boardwalk located along Jeffery Court, Agnes Water. The boardwalk is to be approximately 90m in length with a width varying between 2.8 - 3.2m, including handrail sections (as required) as detailed in this scope of work. The design shall insure that static electricity buildup across the boardwalk and load bearing members and foundation is adequately addressed. The contractor is responsible for the full design, RPEQ engineering certification, construction, site supervision and provision of as constructed drawings upon completion. '

The boardwalk must be designed and built to retain the existing trees, including avoiding damage to the trunks, roots and critical root zones as defined throughout this document. The project also includes the design and installation of xeric (low-water, drought tolerant) coastal landscaping to enhance amenity and provide a low maintenance interface around the boardwalk. The landscaping must be designed to thrive without irrigation.

As an alternative offer, the Contractor may provide a price for the Design and Construct of the new boardwalk utilising alternative composite materials (such as APR). Where such an alternative offer is presented, the contractor shall ensure that static electricity buildup across the boardwalk surface and load bearing members and foundation is adequately addressed.

title: MNHHS200260 TPCH and RBWH Transit Lounge - Principal Contractor
description:
Metro North Health (MNH) is expanding and refurbishing the Transit Lounge at The Prince Charles Hospital (TPCH) and the Discharge Transit Centre at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital (RBWH) to improve patient flow, support timely discharge and provide permanent, contemporary facilities.

The projects will increase TPCH’s capacity from 16 to 24 treatment spaces and RBWH’s capacity from 29 to a minimum of 46 treatment spaces.

Metro North Health is seeking to engage a suitably qualified and experienced construction Tenderer/s to deliver the projects in accordance with the Principal’s approved design documentation, project requirements and applicable statutory and healthcare standards.

Tenderers may submit an offer for either project or both. Each project will be evaluated separately, and MNH may appoint one Contractor for both projects or a separate Contractor for each. Tenderers offering both projects must identify whether they can deliver them concurrently or can accept an award for only one project.

title: Heritage Consultancy Services Panel
description:
The City of Boroondara (the City) is located in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, between 5 and 10 kilometres east of the Melbourne CBD. It is recognised as one of Victoria’s most significant heritage municipalities, containing an extensive and diverse collection of heritage places that reflect the enduring cultural heritage of the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung people as the Traditional Owners and its colonial and multicultural history.

Boroondara’s heritage is shaped by the enduring traditions and places of Aboriginal cultural heritage significance, natural heritage, the rich legacy of 19th century settlement and development, and the ongoing contributions of successive generations of diverse communities.

Boroondara City Council (Council) invites submissions from suitably qualified and experienced heritage consultants for appointment to its Heritage Consultancy Services Panel.

The Panel will comprise approximately six (6) Consultants who may be invited to submit quotations for heritage consultancy services during the term of the Contract.

The Panel will provide Council with timely access to specialist heritage expertise in support of its strategic heritage work program and broader heritage objectives.

Appointment to the Panel does not guarantee a minimum volume of work. Consultants will be engaged on a project-by-project basis, with appointments determined according to the specific requirements of each project, including the consultant’s expertise, capacity, availability, and any other relevant considerations.

Consultants appointed to the Panel may be engaged to deliver a range of strategic heritage services, largely associated with the implementation of Council’s Heritage Strategy 2025-2041 and associated Action Plans, including but not limited to undertaking heritage assessments and preparing citation reports (including those associated with Boroondara’s Community Heritage Nomination Process), preparing and presenting expert evidence for Planning Panels, reviewing and advising on heritage policy matters and other heritage advisory services as required.

publicQuestions.question:
Would Council accept an operator-led EOI where the proposed delivery model involves a third-party property developer or investor funding and delivering the base building, with the operator entering into a long-term lease?

If the developer or investor has not been appointed at the EOI stage, what minimum evidence of operator commitment, financial capacity and the proposed delivery model would Council require?
publicQuestions.answer:
Where a developer or investor has not yet been formally appointed at the EOI stage, Council does not expect respondents to have all project partners fully committed. However, proponents should provide sufficient information to allow Council to assess the credibility and deliverability of the proposal. This may include:

•	A clear description of the proposed delivery and commercial model, including the anticipated roles and responsibilities of the operator and future development/funding partner.

•	Evidence of the operator's commitment to the proposal, including relevant experience, capability, operational track record and intended level of involvement.

•	Information demonstrating the operator's financial capacity to establish and sustain the proposed operation.

•	Details of any discussions, market sounding, expressions of interest, or indicative support received from potential development, investment or funding partners.

•	An outline of the proposed procurement, partnership or investor engagement strategy and indicative timeframes for securing those parties.

•	A commitment to deliver within a reasonable timeline.

•	Any other information that demonstrates the overall feasibility and deliverability of the proposal.

Council will assess proposals based on the information provided and recognises that some aspects of the delivery model may continue to evolve beyond the EOI stage. Shortlisted proponents may be invited to provide further detail, clarification, or supporting information as part of any subsequent stage of the process.

publicQuestions.question:
Pre-lodgement meeting requirements and access to site information

We are working to develop a proposal for the Loganholme Tourism Precinct EOI. At this stage, we have limited site-specific information available to inform concept plans.

Could Council please clarify:

1. Can we book a pre-lodgement meeting to discuss our proposed use and facility requirements before preparing site plans?

2. What minimum information or documentation would Council require for that meeting, particularly in the context of the EOI?

3. How can we access available site information, including surveys, site boundaries, infrastructure details and known development constraints, if available?

4. Where site information is not yet available, would a preliminary concept outlining our proposed activities, space requirements and community benefits be sufficient for an initial discussion at a pre-lodgement meeting?

We would appreciate guidance on the appropriate next step so we can prepare material at the level of detail Council expects.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Can we book a pre-lodgement meeting to discuss our proposed use and facility requirements before preparing site plans?

Yes. Respondents are encouraged to seek pre-lodgement advice to discuss their proposed use, development intent and any planning considerations relevant to the site. A pre-lodgement meeting may be requested before detailed site plans have been prepared. Council notes that, as outlined in the EOI documentation, a pre-lodgement meeting, or at a minimum submission of a request for a pre-lodgement meeting prior to the EOI closing date, is a mandatory requirement of the EOI process. To book a pre-lodgement meeting, please refer to Council’s website - https://www.logan.qld.gov.au/planning-and-building/planning-and-development/development-in-logan/pre-lodgement-advice

2. What minimum information or documentation would Council require for that meeting, particularly in the context of the EOI?

Council does not prescribe a specific format or minimum level of documentation for a pre-lodgement meeting associated with this EOI. However, respondents are encouraged to provide sufficient information to describe their proposed use, development concept, intended activities, facility requirements and any key matters on which guidance is sought. The level of information provided is at the respondent's discretion and should be appropriate to the stage of concept development.

3. How can we access available site information, including surveys, site boundaries, infrastructure details and known development constraints, if available?

Respondents should review the supporting information made available through the EOI process, including the information published on the project website (refer https://loed.com.au/invest/expressions-of-interest-two-prominent-development-sites-in-logan/) and within the EOI documentation. Additional site-specific information may be discussed during a pre-lodgement meeting where available. Respondents are responsible for undertaking their own investigations and due diligence to satisfy themselves regarding site conditions, constraints, opportunities and suitability for their proposed use.

4. Where site information is not yet available, would a preliminary concept outlining our proposed activities, space requirements and community benefits be sufficient for an initial discussion at a pre-lodgement meeting?

Yes. Where detailed site investigations or technical information are not available, a preliminary concept outlining the proposed activities, intended outcomes, facility or land requirements, and anticipated community, social and/or economic benefits would generally be suitable to support an initial pre-lodgement discussion. The purpose of the pre-lodgement process is to enable respondents to seek preliminary feedback and better understand planning and development considerations relevant to their proposal.

We would appreciate guidance on the appropriate next step so we can prepare material at the level of detail Council expects.

Respondents wishing to seek pre-lodgement advice should submit a pre-lodgement meeting request through Council's pre-lodgement process as early as possible. As noted in the EOI documentation, a pre-lodgement meeting must be completed, or at a minimum requested, before the EOI closing date in order to satisfy the mandatory EOI requirement.

publicQuestions.question:
1. Question

Are subdivisions required/expected for the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base?

Background / Context

Does Council require the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base to be managed separately from the balance of the land/lots on which they are to be located, thereby requiring reconfiguration of a lot to establish separate title?

2. Question

Does Council consider the construction (operational works) of any section of the proposed walking track network to constitute assessable development under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016, noting that portions of the proposed alignment are located within flood prone land or land below 20 meters AHD?

Background / Context

Based on the preliminary walking track alignments shown in the Palm Island Track Network Report (Tricky Tracks, January 2026), sections which are expected to require heavy and moderate construction are indicatively:

* Proposed on land located below 20mAHD; and

* within land subject to flooding and/or prone to erosion as identified on overlay maps OM 1 to 4.2.   

Relevantly, under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016, operational works are impact assessable to the extent the works are within floodplain, erosion-prone or coastal hazard areas, or involve specified excavation and fill thresholds below 20m AHD.

3. Question

Does Council have better or more accurate overlay mapping (particularly floodplain and erosion-prone mapping) for the walking track alignments?

Background / Context

The planning scheme overlay mapping is not sufficiently detailed to confirm whether all sections of the proposed walking tracks are subject to flooding and/or erosion constraints.

4. Question

Does Council consider the walking tracks to be operational works under the Palm Island Planning Scheme 2016 and the Planning Act 2016, or are the walking tracks considered to be a material change of use (or both)?

Background / Context

The construction of a walking track is usually not a material change of use. Walking tracks are more commonly defined and assessed as operational works where construction involves earthworks, vegetation clearing or other physical alterations to land.

 The planning scheme definition of Environment Facility includes walking tracks as an example land use. Accordingly, does Council consider the establishment of the proposed walking tracks a material change of use for Environment Facility and operational works (or both)?

5. Question

Does Council agree that the land use for the Cultural Welcome Precinct is "Park"

Background / Context

Under the planning scheme land use definitions, a community use involves the use of premises for providing artistic, social or cultural facilities, or community services, to the public. The examples provided, namely an art gallery, community centre, community hall, library and museum, all share the common characteristic of being identifiable facilities used for the delivery of cultural, social or community functions.

However, while the Cultural Welcome Precinct incorporates cultural expression, interpretation and opportunities for gathering, its primary purpose is not considered to be the provision of a dedicated artistic, social or cultural facility or community service. Rather, it functions as an openly accessible public realm space that facilitates informal recreation, gathering, movement and cultural recognition. The precinct is not intended to operate as a gallery, museum, community centre, performance venue or other comparable facility through which cultural or community services are provided.

The embedded cultural features of the precinct are therefore ancillary to its broader role as park (as defined in the Palm Island Planning Scheme).

Accordingly, the land use is considered to be characterised as a “Park” than as premises used for providing artistic, social or cultural facilities or community services to the public, as contemplated by the definition of community use.

6. Question

Does Council agree that under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, the land use for the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base is Nature-based tourism?

Background / Context

If so, the establishment of the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base is code assessable development under the Palm Island Planning Scheme, within the Family Camp Precinct; otherwise, impact assessment may apply.

7. Question

In the event that any component of the project is determined to constitute assessable development under the Planning Act 2016 requiring a development permit (and assuming no referral agencies are involved), would Council be willing to consider issuing an exemption certificate under section 46 of the Planning Act 2016?

Background / Context

Council may issue an exemption certificate pursuant to (and subject to satisfying the requirements of) s46 of the Planning Act.

8. Question

Could Council advise whether it or the Minggamingga Rangers hold any existing flora, fauna or vegetation data for the island? 

Background / Context

Understanding this will help size the investigations allowance in Item 2 of the Pricing Schedule
publicQuestions.answer:
Answer to Question 1

Council does not currently require or expect separate lots or titles for the walking tracks, Cultural Welcome Precinct or Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base as part of the D&C scope.

The assets may remain within the existing land tenure arrangements. Any future lease, licence, concession or commercial operating arrangement will be considered separately by Council and will remain subject to applicable planning, land tenure, Native Title and ILUA requirements.

Answer to Question 2

The walking-track project includes operational work associated with the physical works; however, Council does not consider the Planning Scheme triggers for floodplain, erosion-prone areas or works below 20 m AHD to make that operational work assessable where the Schedule 6, section 8 public-sector-entity provision applies.

Separate State-level approvals may still apply depending on the final design and alignment, including for coastal, tidal, marine plant, vegetation or waterway matters.

Answer to Question 3

For coastal erosion, Council has more recent coastal-hazard information, including revised erosion-prone area mapping that reflects the protection provided by existing seawalls and reduces the mapped erosion hazard in parts of the township foreshore.

Council does not currently have equivalent refined flood/overland-flow modelling; further modelling has been recommended.

The July 2026 First Nations Coastal Hazard Study – Asset Exposure and Recommendations Final Report will be issued separately by addendum and will replace the previous version included in the procurement documentation.

Answer to Question 4

Both aspects are relevant.

The walking-track project includes an operational-work component associated with the physical works. As outlined in the response to Question 2, Council does not consider that component assessable solely because of the local Planning Scheme operational-work triggers where the Schedule 6 public-sector-entity provision applies.

Separately, the Planning Scheme expressly identifies walking tracks as an Environment facility. Council therefore considers establishment of the walking-track use to constitute a material change of use for an Environment facility, with the applicable assessment pathway determined by the relevant zones and overlays.

Answer to Question 5

Council considers the Cultural Welcome Precinct, as currently proposed, to be principally a Community use under the Planning Scheme.

The proposed cultural performance, interpretation, gallery, artist/maker, visitor orientation and community gathering functions align with that use, with associated amenities, catering and incidental sale of local art and cultural products treated as ancillary activities.

Answer to Question 6

Based on the currently proposed scope, Council's preliminary view is that Nature-based tourism is the most appropriate land-use classification for the Eco-accommodation / Tourism Accommodation Base.

The Planning Scheme definition of Nature-based tourism expressly extends to tourist and visitor short-term accommodation intended to support appreciation of environmental, cultural or heritage values and identifies accommodation such as lodges, cabins, huts and tented camps as examples. This is closely aligned with the proposed low-impact eco-accommodation concept.

Answer to Question 7

Council does not propose to rely on an exemption certificate for the core MCU or overall project. The Walking Trails and Cultural Welcome Precinct comprise substantive new tourism and cultural development, including new trails, visitor facilities, an amphitheatre, cultural and artist spaces, gathering areas and associated infrastructure. Given the project scope, Council does not consider it appropriate to characterise the effects of the whole MCU as minor or inconsequential for the purposes of section 46.

Where operational work is already not assessable under the Schedule 6 public-sector provision, no exemption certificate would be required. Council may, however, consider a section 46 exemption certificate for discrete, low-impact works where the statutory criteria are satisfied.

Answer to Question 8

Council is not in a position to provide any additional site-specific flora, fauna or vegetation datasets beyond the information already included in the procurement documentation.

The Principal Contractor will be responsible for obtaining and verifying all environmental information required for detailed design, approvals and construction, including relevant desktop searches, field investigations and specialist flora/fauna/vegetation surveys. Tenderers should make appropriate allowance for these activities in their submissions.

publicQuestions.question:
Following our review of the tender documents, we seek clarification regarding the specification and testing requirements applicable to the requested cold-mix asphalt product.

1. Applicable Specification

The tender noted compliance with MRTS02, MRTS12, MRTS21. Please note, MRTS02 - Provision for Traffic, MRTS12 - Sprayed Bituminous Emulsion Surfacing and MRTS21 - Bituminous Emulsion. How are these specifications applicable to this tender?

As the request is for the supply of cold-mix asphalt, could Council please confirm the specific TMR specification or performance requirements intended to apply to the product, as MRTS30 is for hot-mix asphalt used in road pavements and is not for the manufacture and storage of cold mix.

MRTS30 contains requirements relating to asphalt manufacture, placement, compaction, in-situ air voids and contractor performance. Could Council clarify whether compliance with the entirety of MRTS30 is required, or only selected material testing requirements?

2. Testing Requirements

The tender references testing in accordance with Q307 and Q308A/Q308C. Please confirm that these testing requirements and frequencies are intended for the nominated cold-mix asphalt product and advise the acceptance criteria to be applied.

3. Product Requirements

To ensure all tenderers are pricing the same product, please provide confirmation of:

i) Nominal aggregate size.

ii) Intended application (pothole repairs, patching, pavement maintenance, etc.).

iii) Required shelf life or stockpile life.

iv) Any minimum performance or durability requirements.

4. Equivalent Products

Will Council consider proprietary cold-mix asphalt products that are widely used for maintenance and patching applications where they satisfy the intended operational requirements but are not specifically designed to meet all MRTS30 construction criteria?
publicQuestions.answer:
1.Compliance Requirements

MTRS requirements are no longer valid as that portion of the tender was dropped.

Testing, materials, workmanship, and performance shall comply with the requirements of the Routine Maintenance Guidelines, Transport and Main Roads, June 2026, specifically Section 111 – Surface Correction with Premix/Asphalt (Mechanical) – Minor (150 m/km), Page 168, for the application of cold-mixed asphalt pavement repairs.

2.Product Requirements

The product shall be suitable for use in Surface Correction with Premix/Asphalt (Mechanical) applications and shall comply with TMR Materials Specification Q309 (Materials/Mix Design). A 14 mm nominal size mix is preferred; however, suppliers may nominate an alternative blend provided it fully complies with the requirements and performance criteria of Section 111 – Surface Correction with Premix/Asphalt (Mechanical) – Minor (150 m/km) of the Routine Maintenance Guidelines. with a stockpile life of 3-4 months

3.Alternative Products

Alternative products and mix designs will be considered where the supplier can demonstrate that the proposed product meets or exceeds the performance, material, and application requirements specified in the Routine Maintenance Guidelines, Transport and Main Roads, June 2026, and any other applicable Transport and Main Roads specifications.

1.	Offshore delivery of design and engineering services. Where a respondent’s in-house engineering team performs design and documentation work outside Australia, with on-site survey work delivered by Australian-based personnel, could the DoE please confirm:

-	whether offshore delivery of design, drafting or engineering services is permitted under the Government Compliance Requirements referenced in mandatory criterion M4, or under any resulting Standing Offer Arrangement (SOA) and

-	whether specific requirements apply to offshore access, storage or processing of customer information e.g. site and floor plans for schools and health facilities etc

2.	Delivery partners not yet under contract (Tab E). Where a respondent has engaged prospective delivery partners who have agreed in principle to participate but are not yet under contract at EOI stage, could the DoE please confirm whether partners in this position may be named in Tab E?

3.	Indicative volumes and distribution of work. To help respondents describe delivery scale and capacity accurately (criterion C3, Tabs C and D), could the DoE please advise:

-	the indicative annual volume of work, by service category where available

-	the expected distribution of work across DoE regions and other participating agencies and

-	whether any SOA will include minimum volume commitments, or whether work will be allocated on an as-required basis

4.	Supply of active equipment. Will DoE and QH normally supply active equipment e.g. switches, routers, wireless access points, with suppliers installing and commissioning only, or are suppliers expected to supply the equipment as well?

5.	OEM platforms. The EOI mentions Aruba, Juniper and Cisco. Are these the current platforms across DoE and QH environments, and are there other platforms in use or planned for which suppliers should hold certifications?

6.	Equipment procurement. Where suppliers are expected to supply equipment, who are the “approved suppliers”? Must equipment be purchased through an existing Queensland Government arrangement (such as a current SOA), or may suppliers purchase directly from the OEM or through their own distribution channels?

7.	Cabling manufacturer accreditation. Would a supplier need to hold Certified Installer accreditation for all five cabling systems named in the EOI (Molex, CommScope, Panduit, Belden and Siemon) to be considered for QH work, or would accreditation with one or more be sufficient?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thanks for your questions, please see below responses:

1. Offshore delivery of design and engineering services:

Offshore delivery models are not prohibited at the EOI stage. Any resulting arrangement would be subject to applicable Queensland Government requirements, including the QITC Standing Offer Arrangement Conditions and Details – ICT Products and Services. Any specific requirements relating to offshore access, storage or processing of customer information would be considered during any subsequent procurement and contracting phase.

2. Delivery partners not yet under contract (Tab E):

Yes. Respondents may identify prospective delivery partners that are not yet under contract, provided the nature and status of the relationship is clearly disclosed in the response.

3. Indicative volumes and distribution of work:

Indicative volumes, geographic distribution or future demand forecasts are not available at this EOI stage. Respondents should describe their current delivery capacity, scalability and maximum capability based on the information provided in the EOI.

No minimum work volumes are being committed through this EOI. Any future contractual arrangements or volume commitments, if applicable, would be considered through subsequent procurement activities.

4. Supply of active equipment:

Both delivery models may occur. Depending on customer requirements, suppliers may be engaged to install customer-supplied equipment or to supply and install equipment as part of a broader solution. Any equipment procurement requirements would be determined by the customer for the relevant procurement activity, work order or engagement.

5. OEM platforms:

The OEMs referenced in the EOI are representative of platforms currently used within participating environments. Respondents should identify all relevant manufacturer accreditations and certifications they currently hold. Certifications beyond those specifically referenced in the EOI may also be relevant and should be included where applicable.

6. Equipment procurement:

Where equipment supply forms part of a requirement, customers may direct suppliers to utilise existing procurement arrangements, customer-nominated suppliers or other sourcing approaches, as appropriate. Specific procurement requirements would be determined by the customer for the relevant engagement.

7. Cabling manufacturer accreditation:

No. Respondents are not required to hold accreditation across all manufacturer platforms referenced in the EOI. Respondents should identify all manufacturer accreditations, authorised installer status and manufacturer warranty capabilities they currently hold. The relevance of particular accreditations may vary depending on customer requirements.

publicQuestions.question:
To assist with accurate and commercially sustainable pricing of the separable portions, could Council please clarify the following:

1. If available, could Council provide indicative annual quantities by activity and separable portion for the initial 12-month term, together with any relevant historical quantities from the previous arrangement? It is acknowledged that any quantities provided would be indicative only and would not constitute a guaranteed volume of work.

2. What is the typical size and duration of an individual work package, and how much mobilisation notice does Council generally provide to the highest-ranked available supplier?

3. Are work packages ordinarily expected to be completed as continuous operations, or may the delivery program be agreed with Council when each package is issued?

4. The Specification requires the contractor to source construction water. Are any Council-controlled water points ordinarily available within the separable portions, and if so, what access, permit or usage charges apply?

5. Please confirm whether the supplied Traffic Management Plan/TGS 21 represents the typical traffic-management arrangement for these activities, or whether requirements will be determined separately for each work package.

6. Given that submitted pricing is fixed for the initial 12-month term, would Council consider a periodic rise-and-fall adjustment applied only to the fuel component of the relevant rates and calculated using the ABS Automotive Fuel Index? Any such adjustment would operate in both directions, providing Council with a corresponding reduction when the index falls. Alternatively, should tenderers incorporate the full fuel-price risk into their fixed rates?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. If available, could Council provide indicative annual quantities by activity and separable portion for the initial 12-month term, together with any relevant historical quantities from the previous arrangement? It is acknowledged that any quantities provided would be indicative only and would not constitute a guaranteed volume of work.

ANSWER:

Council is not able to provide indicative annual quantities by activity or separable portion for the initial 12-month term, nor historical quantities from the previous arrangement. Tenderers should base their pricing and resourcing proposals on the scope of works, specifications, and any other information provided within the tender documentation. Actual volumes of work will vary according to operational need, budget allocations, weather events, and Council priorities during the contract term, and will be issued progressively.

2. What is the typical size and duration of an individual work package, and how much mobilisation notice does Council generally provide to the highest-ranked available supplier?

ANSWER:

Work packages vary in size and duration so there is no typical size allocated. Packages are no less than 500m. Mobilisation notice is generally required within 2-4 weeks depending on operational need.

3. Are work packages ordinarily expected to be completed as continuous operations, or may the delivery program be agreed with Council when each package is issued?

ANSWER:

The delivery program will be discussed and agreed with Council at the time of engagement for each work package.

4. The Specification requires the contractor to source construction water. Are any Council-controlled water points ordinarily available within the separable portions, and if so, what access, permit or usage charges apply?

ANSWER:

Council has a limited number of Council-controlled water points (bores/dams) that may be available, details will be discussed at the time of engagement. Council does not charge for access to its own water points for operational needs. Where a contractor sources water from a private party, any associated charges will be the contractor's responsibility.

5. Please confirm whether the supplied Traffic Management Plan/TGS 21 represents the typical traffic-management arrangement for these activities, or whether requirements will be determined separately for each work package.

ANSWER:

The supplied TGS is generic in nature. The preferred contractor may be asked to provide a more specific TGS suited to a particular activity, as required.

6. Given that submitted pricing is fixed for the initial 12-month term, would Council consider a periodic rise-and-fall adjustment applied only to the fuel component of the relevant rates and calculated using the ABS Automotive Fuel Index? Any such adjustment would operate in both directions, providing Council with a corresponding reduction when the index falls. Alternatively, should tenderers incorporate the full fuel-price risk into their fixed rates?

ANSWER:

The most recent escalations of fuel pricing has made the ideal of fixing prices for the intitial term difficult for tenderers to be able to price in the risk of further escalations. Undertaking frequent rise and fall reviews will also be too onerous. Therefore, Council will instead seek pricing for each discrete parcel of work from the panel of providers, when and as the work is required. The selection criteria and weightings will still apply in determining the rankings. The evaluation panel will score the tender responses, and these scores will carry forward throughout the life of the panel arrangement to be applied for each discrete requirement. Tenderers will not be required to provide pricing initially to be assessed for inclusion to the panel (Annexure A Pricing Schedule and section 3.2 of the Response schedule), however Council may request this information from Panellists at a later date should fuel settle and become more predictable.

title: Processing of Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) Material from kerbside organic bin collection
description:
Ballina Shire Council is seeking tenders from suitably experienced and qualified Service Providers to accept and process all Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) material collected through its kerbside organic bin collection service, at a licenced organics processing facility (OPF). The proposed contract comprises an initial term of five (5) years, with three (3) further options of one (1) year each, exercisable by Council at its sole discretion.

Council also accepts self-hauled household and commercial Garden Organics (GO) at the Ballina Resource Recovery Centre, which is currently processed by a local contractor. The scope of this Contract includes provision for the processing of that material if the existing arrangement ceases during the Contract term.

In a separate file, please provide valid Certificates of Currency for the following insurances:

- Public Liability Insurance – minimum $20 million
- NSW Workers Compensation Insurance
- Comprehensive Motor Vehicle and Plant Insurance

Where the tenderer holds Environmental impairment liability (pollution liability) insurance, it may provide a certificate of currency. If the tenderer does not presently hold such insurance, it may provide details demonstrating its ability to obtain appropriate cover.

This insurance though, whilst highly regarded, is not mandatory.

In a separate document, please demonstrate your current :

- WHS Management System
- Environmental Management System
- Quality Management System

Please also provide copies of any accreditations held for these systems.
Please submit a copy of your Current Environment Protection Licence (EPL) authorising the receipt and processing of commingled recyclables as issued by the NSW EPA,

In a separate document, please provide details around the following aspects of service:

- Residual Waste: Identify each facility proposed to receive Residual Waste, including its location, operator and applicable licence or approval.

- Resources and Personnel: Describe the management, staffing, plant, equipment, systems and other resources proposed to perform the Services and maintain continuity throughout the Term.

- Resource Recovery: State the resource recovery target proposed under clause 1.3.18 of the Specification and explain the methodology by which the Tenderer proposes to achieve, measure and report against that target.

- Service Performance: Describe the Tenderer’s proposed approach to monitoring and meeting the KPIs, reporting requirements and continuous-improvement obligations under the Contract.

- Commencement: Describe the Tenderer’s proposed mobilisation and implementation arrangements to ensure readiness to commence the Services on 1 July 2027.

Please provide details of any subcontractor proposed to perform a material part of the Services. If no material subcontracting is proposed, state “None”.

Where the OPF or an Alternative Facility is owned or operated by another person who will perform any part of the Services, that person must be identified in this Schedule.

For each proposed subcontractor, provide sufficient information to enable Council to assess its relevant experience, capability and regulatory standing and, where requested, details of relevant insurance and references.

Nomination of a subcontractor does not constitute approval by Council. Any subcontracting under the Contract remains subject to clause 18 of the Conditions of Contract.

In a separate document, describe the social and community benefits associated with the Tenderer’s proposed delivery of the Services.

The response should address:
•	the Tenderer’s knowledge of and experience operating in Ballina Shire, the Northern Rivers or comparable regional areas;
•	anticipated benefits to the local and regional economy arising from performance of the Contract;
•	the extent to which the Tenderer proposes to utilise local employment, suppliers, contractors or services in performing the Contract; and
•	any other specific and measurable social or community benefits the Tenderer commits to delivering if successful.

Tenderers should distinguish existing business activities from additional commitments proposed specifically in connection with this Contract.

vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription:
** ABOUT THE BEGA VALLEY **

The Bega Valley Shire is located at the south-eastern corner of New South Wales, halfway between Australia’s two largest cities, Sydney and Melbourne and three hours’ drive from the nation’s capital, Canberra.

Our coastal fringe extends from Wallaga Lake in the north to Cape Howe and the Victorian border in the south. Collectively this 225-kilometre section forms the beautiful Sapphire Coast, the heart of Australia’s Coastal Wilderness.

Our community vision explains our collective aspiration that we are an inclusive and welcoming community that integrates quality of life, prosperity, sustainable development and conservation of the environment. Our connection to Country is guided by the culture and heritage of our Traditional Owners.

** ABOUT COUNCIL **

Bega Valley Shire Council is responsible for providing all of the typical local government services across the Bega Valley Shire including maintaining a broad range of assets valued at over $1.7 billion that allow our visitors and community alike to live, work and play.

The Bega Valley Shire is governed by an elected Council comprising nine Councillors. Councillors provide leadership and establish policy and strategic direction for the organisation and the future of the shire.

Delivering the day to day services for council is a professional and dynamic staff cohort of over 560 people including full time, contract and casual positions.

Contractors to council play an important and valued role, assisting us delivering services and projects to the highest of standards and value for money.

** WHAT COUNCIL DOES **

Provide and maintain community facilities such as:
•	Parks and sportsgrounds
•	Playgrounds and skate parks
•	Sapphire Aquatic centre Pambula and swimming pools throughout the shire
•	Sports and recreation facilities throughout the Shire
•	Local libraries in Bega, Bermagui, Eden and Merimbula
•	Preschools and Childcare centres in Bega and Eden, and our Mobile service for Candelo and Bemboka
•	Merimbula Airport, Bega Saleyards and Cemeteries throughout the Shire

We care for the environment by:
•	Managing and enhancing bushland areas
•	Providing environmental and waste education and recycling services
•	Responding to pollution incidents and prosecuting polluters
•	Monitoring the water quality of the Shire’s estuaries
•	Planting trees and controlling noxious weeds
•	Beneficially recycling and reusing treated effluent

We create a safer place to live by:
•	Maintaining and improving roads, footpaths and stormwater drains
•	Working with emergency organisations such as the Rural Fire Service, State Emergency Service, NSW Police and NSW Surf Life Saving
•	Managing the keeping of companion animals
•	Inspecting food premises
•	Treating and supplying drinking water to our community
•	Treating sewage to a high standard to protect human health

We enhance our community by:
•	Listening to community views
•	Holding citizenship ceremonies, Australia Day Celebrations and the Seniors week luncheon known as the Golden Gig
•	Offering services for seniors, young people, new migrants and people with a disability
•	Providing grants to community organisations
•	Supporting local community groups such as sporting clubs, arts, migrant groups and charities
•	Encouraging and promoting volunteering in our communities

We plan for the future by:
•	Planning and managing the urban environment
•	Preserving heritage sites
•	Consulting with the community about its needs
•	Developing long term strategic plans for Council and the Shire
